about: Every string the spelling map changed while building the Brennan's house: the research writes British English and the house is American, so each British form became its American spelling.

changes.before: The fourth course is the steak, the last savoury course before the Bananas Foster, and the one a grand New Orleans breakfast has always included. It is a petite filet mignon, the most tender cut, cooked to the temperature you chose with your order, beside a potato rösti, RUHSH-tee, a Swiss-style cake of shredded potato fried golden and crisp, and garlic spinach. The plate is simple: tender, beefy and clean, with crunch from the rösti and garlic from the spinach. We pour a four-ounce glass of Domaine de Châteaumar ‘Cuvée Vincent’ Côtes du Rhône with it, juicy, soft and just right for red meat in the morning.

changes.before: Our fourth course on the Dinner Tasting Menu is Roasted Rohan Duck Breast, and duck with fruit is a French classic done the Louisiana way. Rohan, ROH-han, is a special cross raised in New York for its tender, rosy meat, and the breast is roasted so the skin renders and the meat stays rosy. The peaches are glazed with cane syrup, Louisiana’s own sugarcane syrup, lighter and more buttery than molasses, so they are sweet with a deep caramel note, and candied hazelnuts add crunch. It tastes rich and savoury against the sweet fruit. On the pairing we pour a Napa Cabernet from Coombsville with it.

changes.before: Our Café Brûlot Coffee Cake is a sweet starter on the breakfast and lunch menu, named for café brûlot, ka-FAY broo-LOH, the classic New Orleans coffee flamed with brandy, orange and lemon peel, cinnamon and clove. The cake borrows those flavours: it’s baked with chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate, then finished with a spiced citrus glaze, which carries the brûlot’s spice, pecans for crunch, and whipped crème fraîche, krem FRESH, a slightly tangy cream that keeps it from being too sweet. It tastes dark, moist and roasty, with orange and warm spice. Share it at the start, or save it for a cup of our coffee with chicory.

changes.before: Our Louisiana Oysters come in New Orleans BBQ sauce, and in New Orleans barbecue doesn’t mean a smoker or a tomato sauce: it’s the style made famous by barbecue shrimp at Pascal’s Manale, Uptown, in the mid-1950s, a rich, buttery sauce with lots of black pepper and savoury Worcestershire. The oysters come warm in that sauce, then we add pickled collard greens for a sharp, bright bite, shallots, and a fried saltine crumble for crunch. It’s rich and peppery, not hot, with a pickled tang and crunch in every bite: a real New Orleans flavour, and a lovely one to share before your eggs.

changes.before: Our Creole Tomato Tostada celebrates Louisiana tomato season. Creole tomatoes are Louisiana’s summer tomato, juicy, sweet and a little tart; we mix them with heirlooms and serve them raw and simply, with creamy burrata, boo-RAH-tuh, fresh mozzarella with a soft, cream-filled centre, cool and rich against the acidity. They sit on a housemade okra tostada, a crisp flat shell made here with okra, and smoked tomato water, a clear, intensely tomatoey broth, is poured around for a whisper of smoke. It’s juicy, sweet-tart and creamy, with crunch and a hint of smoke: light, seasonal and gone when the tomatoes are, so order it while it’s here.

changes.before: Our Louisiana Crab Claws are a local favourite: sweet, delicate crab meat you pick up and eat off the claw. They come warm, dressed in a brown butter vinaigrette, butter cooked until it turns nutty and toasty, then balanced with acidity so it’s rich but bright. Fines herbes, feen ZAIRB, the classic French mix of parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, finish them with a soft, fresh green note. Use the pincer as a handle, bite, and slide the cartilage out; we bring a plate for the shells and napkins. It tastes of sweet crab, nutty butter, bright acid and soft herbs: simple, elegant and lovely to share.

changes.before: Our Steak Tartare Cannoli is raw, finely chopped beef in a crisp potato shell shaped like a cannoli, with crème fraîche and a cured egg yolk grated over the top like bottarga: cool, silky and savoury in a crunchy shell.

changes.before: Our Steak Tartare Cannoli is a playful take on steak tartare, tar-TAR: raw beef, finely chopped and seasoned, and instead of toast we pipe it into a potato cannoli, a crisp potato shell shaped like the pastry, so it’s savoury, not sweet. Crème fraîche, krem FRESH, a tangy cultured cream, keeps the beef cool and silky. The egg yolk bottarga, boh-TAR-gah, is an egg yolk cured until firm and grated over the top the way Italians grate bottarga, cured fish roe, for a rich, salty finish. It’s handheld, two or three bites. If you like steak tartare, this is a fun way to start dinner.

changes.before: Our Turtle Soup is a Brennan’s classic and one of the great Creole soups, rich and long-cooked. It’s made with 100% turtle meat, farm raised Louisiana freshwater turtle; many turtle soups are stretched with veal or beef, and ours is all turtle. It’s deep and savoury: if you’ve never had turtle, think of a rich, finely chopped stew. Brown butter spinach adds a toasty, earthy note, the grated egg adds richness, and a splash of aged Sherry brings a nutty, dry lift that cuts the richness. It’s the soup on our Traditional Breakfast, and if you want one bowl that tells you what Brennan’s is about, this is it.

changes.before: Our Seafood Gumbo is a Brennan’s signature, and gumbo, GUM-boh, is the dish that says Louisiana: a Creole stew built on a roux. Ours is all about the seafood, shrimp, crab and oysters, so you get sweetness and a little brine in every spoonful. Andouille, ahn-DOO-ee, a coarse, smoked Cajun pork sausage, gives it a savoury, smoky backbone and a gentle warmth. It’s served over popcorn rice, a Louisiana long-grain with a nutty, toasty aroma that really does smell a little like popcorn. It’s hearty, so it’s a great start before one of the egg dishes, and it’s the other soup choice on our Traditional Breakfast.

changes.before: Our Creole Caesar is a Louisiana take on a Caesar. Gem lettuce is small, sweet and very crisp, so it holds up to a creamy dressing, and ours is a smoked oyster dressing: the smoked oysters bring the deep, savoury flavour a Caesar is known for, with a smoky edge. Grana Padano, GRAH-nah pah-DAH-noh, a nutty Italian hard cheese much like Parmesan, adds salt and richness, and the crisps are made from bread by Leidenheimer, LY-den-hy-mer, the bakery behind New Orleans’ po-boy loaf since 1896. It tastes crisp, creamy, smoky and savoury. It’s a great, lighter start before an egg dish or the redfish.

changes.before: Eggs Hussarde is our signature egg dish: poached eggs and coffee-cured Canadian bacon on housemade English muffins, with two sauces, hollandaise and marchand de vin, a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce. Rich and buttery, with a bright, lemony edge and a deep, winey note.

changes.before: Eggs Hussarde is our signature egg dish, the New Orleans cousin of Eggs Benedict. We make our own English muffins, and the Canadian bacon is cured with coffee, so it's smoky and a little roasty; the poached eggs go on top with two sauces, marchand de vin, the wine merchant's sauce, a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce, and hollandaise, the buttery, lemony one. The dish is older than the restaurant, but we made it famous from about 1950. Rich, savoury and bright, and the heart of our Traditional Breakfast: if it's your first breakfast with us, this is the one.

changes.before: Eggs Owen is our heartiest egg dish. It sits over a Creole-spiced potato with a soft-boiled egg, so the yolk runs into everything, under the same two sauces as our Hussarde: hollandaise for richness, and marchand de vin, a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce that echoes the braise. changes.before: Our Duck Confit Waffle is chicken and waffles gone luxurious. The duck is a Rohan duck leg made as confit, kohn-FEE: cured and cooked slowly in its own fat until it's tender, with crisp skin. It sits on a savoury cornbread and chive waffle, and foie gras butter melts in for extra richness. Mustard maple syrup brings sweetness with a little tang to balance all that, and a sunny-side-up egg ties it together. Crisp, rich and savoury-sweet, the maple and mustard cutting the duck and the butter. It's a rich plate, so I'd keep the starter light: a showstopper for a brunch guest who wants something different.

changes.before: Our Pecan Gulf Fish is the day's catch from the Gulf, cooked to order; the fish changes with what the boats bring, and I can tell you what it is today. It's topped with Louisiana lump crab, the sweet, meaty pieces from the body of the blue crab, and Louisiana lands more blue crab than any other state. The sauce is a pecan bordelaise, bor-duh-LAYZ, nutty and savoury. Underneath sit a silky cauliflower purée and wilted collard greens, which bring a little earthiness. Nutty and buttery, sweet from the crab: lighter than the egg dishes but still satisfying, the plate for a guest who wants fish at midday.

changes.before: Our Crab & Corn Omelette is a summer-in-Louisiana omelette, and the egg dish for a guest who doesn't want hollandaise. Louisiana lump crab and roasted sweet corn are both naturally sweet, so they belong together, folded into the eggs. Our house-made miso butter adds a savoury, almost nutty depth, and lemon and basil keep it fresh. On top goes a gremolata, greh-moh-LAH-tah, an Italian mix of herbs and citrus zest, made with Marcona almonds, the rich, tender Spanish almonds. Sweet, buttery and savoury, with a bright, herbal crunch. If you love crab, this is the one: the lighter choice that still feels special.

changes.before: This is steak and eggs done properly, our breakfast and lunch steak. Hanger is the butcher's favourite cut, loose-grained and beefy; ours is Black Angus from Creekstone Farms in Kansas, graded Prime, which is unusual for a hanger, and seasoned with Creole spice. The smoked potato pavé is thin potato slices layered, pressed and crisped, with a smoky note. A sunny-side-up Vital Farms egg, pasture-raised, gives you a runny yolk, and French béarnaise, the tarragon butter sauce, is the classic match for steak. Beefy and spiced, with crisp layered potato and a rich sauce. It's at its best medium-rare to medium, so tell me how you'd like it cooked.

changes.before: The Roasted Chateaubriand serves two: the thick centre of a Creekstone Farms beef tenderloin, roasted whole, with roasted and glazed summer squash and sauce Foyot, a béarnaise enriched with meat glaze. Very tender and buttery, with a rich, savoury sauce.

changes.before: Chateaubriand, shah-toh-bree-AHN, is the classic French cut for two: the thick, tender centre of the beef tenderloin, roasted whole so it stays juicy, and named, the story goes, for the Vicomte de Chateaubriand. Ours is Creekstone Farms Black Angus beef. Tenderloin is lean and mild, so the sauce does the work: Foyot, fwah-YO, is béarnaise, the tarragon butter sauce, made even richer with a reduced meat glaze. Roasted and glazed summer squash keeps it light. Very tender and buttery, with a rich, savoury sauce. It's our celebration plate for two; a whole roast takes longer, and a side of Maggie's Mushrooms or Shells & Cheese makes it a feast.

changes.before: It's where a French bistro meets a Southern kitchen. Poussin, poo-SAN, is a young, small chicken; ours is a Cornish hen, and it comes whole, so it may have bones. We brine it in sweet tea, a Southern fried chicken trick that seasons it and keeps it juicy, then fry it until the skin is crisp. The sauce is the French half: poulet à la moutarde is a Burgundian bistro classic, and our mustard cream sauce is tangy and rich, with turnips and shallots for a gentle sweetness. Crisp, juicy and savoury, with a tangy, creamy sauce. If you love fried chicken, you'll love this.

changes.before: Our Blackened Tofu is local Tien Dat tofu, crusted with blackening spices and seared, over creamy Two Brooks Farm rice grits with preserved shiitake mushrooms. Spiced and crusty outside, soft inside, with earthy, savoury mushrooms.
changes.after: Our Blackened Tofu is local Tien Dat tofu, crusted with blackening spices and seared, over creamy Two Brooks Farm rice grits with preserved shiitake mushrooms. Spiced and crusty outside, soft inside, with earthy, savory mushrooms.

changes.before: There's no meat on its menu line, and it's full of flavour. The tofu is Tien Dat, the menu's New Orleans tofu, made fresh across the river by a local Vietnamese American maker. We blacken it, the Louisiana technique Paul Prudhomme made famous around 1980: coated in spices and seared in a very hot pan, so it gets a dark, spiced crust. Under it, rice grits from Two Brooks Farm in the Mississippi Delta, broken rice cooked creamy like grits, and preserved shiitake mushrooms, shee-TAH-kee, for deep, savoury flavour. Spiced and crusty outside, soft inside, with earthy, savoury mushrooms and moderate spice; you won't miss the meat.

Chili crisp, the crunchy Chinese chili oil, brings real heat. A French garnish, a Mexican seed and a Chinese condiment on a Creole-spiced steak: that mix is the modern Brennan's style. Beefy and spiced, with crunch, heat and a sweet-savoury glaze. It's at its best medium-rare to medium; how do you like your steak?

changes.before:
The Swordfish Grenobloise is a fall dinner entrée from the Fall 2026 menu; the sheet prints no price, so ask a manager before quoting one.

Grenobloise, gruh-no-BLWAZ, means of Grenoble, and in the kitchen it is a treatment rather than a fish: brown butter, lemon and capers, with parsley and usually croutons, classically on sole. Here it goes on a swordfish fillet, a firm, meaty, mildly sweet fish, so describe it with confidence. With the fish comes a leek fondue, fon-DOO, leeks cooked slowly in butter until they melt soft and sweet; it is not a cheese fondue. The butter is cooked to the colour of hazelnuts, the lemon cuts the richness, the capers are fried so they crisp and pop with salt, and the croutons are cut from Leidenheimer, the New Orleans French bread baked since 1896.

The guest sees the fillet, the soft leeks, the capers, parsley and croutons, glossed with the butter. It tastes rich and nutty, bright with lemon, salty from the capers, with soft leeks and crunch. The Gainey Chardonnay is the pour, creamy enough for the brown butter and fresh enough for the lemon.

Chateaubriand, shah-toh-bree-AHN, is the thick centre cut of the beef tenderloin, the most tender cut on the animal and a lean one, and ours is a twelve-ounce cut. Lean beef wants a sauce with depth, and this one gets Espagnole, ess-pan-YOL, one of the classical French mother sauces: brown stock thickened with a brown roux, with tomato and aromatic vegetables, simmered long and skimmed until it is glossy and deep. It is savoury rather than tomatoey. Beside it come frascarelli, frah-skah-REL-lee, small rustic pasta pieces with roots in the Marche in central Italy; the sheet describes flour and egg loosely combined into irregular pieces, boiled and finished in butter.

The guest gets tender, lean beef under a glossy brown sauce and soft, buttery pasta: comfort with a classical backbone. The sheet prints no cooking method and no serving count, so learn both at lineup. I'd pour the Moulin d'Issan Bordeaux Supérieur with it, polished tannin for the beef and cedar for the sauce.

Agnolotti del plin, ah-nyoh-LOT-tee del PLEEN, are the small pinched pasta parcels of Piedmont, from the Langhe hills around Alba. Plin means a pinch in the local dialect: a sheet of pasta is folded over small portions of filling and pinched shut between them, so each parcel carries the mark of a thumb and a finger. In Piedmont the fillings vary, meat and vegetable both. Ours sets the parcels with pork, braised collards, ricotta and Parmesan, and finishes the plate with lemon pangrattato, pahn-graht-TAH-toh, crisp breadcrumbs with lemon. The sheet lists the six parts and does not say which sit inside the pasta and which around it, so learn the build at lineup before you describe the filling.

It eats tender and savoury: soft pasta, pork, sweet and earthy greens, creamy ricotta and salty Parmesan, then the lemon crunch. The Barbera d'Asti is the pour, a Piedmont red with the acidity for the cheese and the fruit for the pork.

Daube, DOHB, is the slow braise of Provence: meat cooked gently in wine and aromatics until a fork turns it. Lamb shank is a working cut from the lower leg, full of connective tissue, and hours of slow, moist heat melt that sinew into gelatin, so the meat turns tender and deeply flavoured. En croûte, ahn KROOT, means in a crust, and here it is puff pastry, which bakes up flaky and crisp around the lamb. With it comes the jus, ZHOO, a spiced lamb jus scented with star anise, orange and a touch of cinnamon.

What the guest gets is soft, savoury lamb inside a crisp shell, and a sauce that smells of fall without heat. The sheet does not say whether the bone comes to the table inside the pastry or how the meat is arranged, so learn the build at lineup before you explain how to eat it. I'd pour the Durban Beaumes-de-Venise, a Southern Rhône red with ripe fruit and warm spice for the jus.

Château Climens 2010 is the sweet spot bottle with the Lemon Tart: bin 192821, $200.

Barsac is the village next to Sauternes in Bordeaux, on lower, limestone ground, and its sweet wines are known for a lifted freshness. Château Climens, klee-MAHNS, is a first growth of Barsac in the 1855 classification of sweet wines, farmed biodynamically. Unusually, it makes its wine from Sémillon alone. The grapes are picked by hand in several passes once noble rot has shrivelled and concentrated them, and the wine is aged in oak.

At sixteen years it is deep gold. It tastes of candied lemon, apricot, pineapple, honey and saffron, sweet and rich, but with a freshness that keeps it lively.

It is on the list as one of the great sweet wines of Bordeaux, and it suits the Lemon Tart because its citrus meets the yuzu and lemon jelly, and its honey loves the toasted meringue.

The pink house at 417 Royal Street was built in 1795, after the great fire, and soon passed to Don José Faurie. It later became the Banque de la Louisiane, the first bank in Louisiana, and the bank's initials, LB, still sit in the ironwork at the centre of the balcony railing.

From 1841 to 1891 the Morphy family owned it, and Paul Morphy, the chess prodigy many called the unofficial world champion, lived there until his death in 1884.

Brennan's has served here since 1956. Guests often ask how old the building is while they wait for the first course, so point them to the balcony monogram on the way out: it is the easiest way to make the history real.

Auguste Escoffier, the chef who codified French restaurant cooking in Le Guide Culinaire (1903), organised sauces into families built on four base sauces: espagnole, velouté, béchamel and tomate. Kitchens now add hollandaise and teach five mother sauces; every other classical sauce is a daughter, built by adding to one of them.

Brennan's menus read like a lesson in the hollandaise family: plain hollandaise on the Hussarde and Owen, béarnaise on the breakfast hanger, Choron on the Sardou, Foyot on the Chateaubriand. The marchand de vin and bordelaise come from the brown side.

The guide's own advice is that the sauce usually matters more than the protein, for the guest and for the wine. Learn the sauce on each plate first and the rest of the description follows.

Marchand de vin means wine merchant. In classical French cooking it is shallots reduced in red wine with a brown stock or demi-glace. New Orleans made its own version: onion and plenty of garlic in place of the shallot, often ham and mushrooms, beef stock and red wine, frequently bound with a roux into a glossy brown sauce. Antoine's made it famous in the city.

The guide's best wording is a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce; calling it a bare reduction undersells it.

On the Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen it is the dark, winey half of the two sauces, under the egg. Whether tonight's sauce carries ham or mushroom is a question for the chef before you promise either.

Sauce Choron is béarnaise finished with tomato. It is named for Alexandre Étienne Choron, chef de cuisine at the celebrated Voisin restaurant on the rue Saint-Honoré in Paris, who is also remembered for the extraordinary Christmas menu he served during the Siege of Paris.

The tomato is cooked down to a thick paste before it is folded in, so it colours the sauce a soft coral and adds a gentle sweetness without thinning the emulsion.

Brennan's puts Choron on the Eggs Sardou in place of the usual hollandaise. The guide's words for it are tangy and herbal, and that is how to say it to a guest: béarnaise with tomato, brighter than hollandaise.

Sauce Foyot, also called sauce Valois, is béarnaise with meat glaze whisked in. Glace de viande is brown stock reduced until it is thick and syrupy; a spoonful turns pale, sharp béarnaise tawny, deeper and more savoury.

It takes its name from the Restaurant Foyot on the rue de Tournon in Paris, opposite the Senate, named for Nicolas Foyot, who had cooked for King Louis-Philippe. Several dishes there carried the house name.

On the Roasted Chateaubriand it does a necessary job: tenderloin is the leanest, mildest cut on the animal, so a rich, savoury sauce brings the depth the meat lacks. Say it as béarnaise made even richer with a reduced beef glaze.

Crème anglaise is the French pouring custard: milk or cream heated with sugar and vanilla, poured over egg yolks, and stirred gently until it coats the back of a spoon, never boiled or it curdles. It is the base of ice cream and of a Bavarian cream.

A roux is flour cooked in fat, stirred constantly, and used to thicken and flavour a sauce or soup. French kitchens cook it white or blond for béchamel and velouté. Louisiana cooks take it much further, to peanut butter, then chocolate or mahogany brown, which gives a toasty, nutty depth; the darker it gets, the more flavour and the less thickening power it has.

A dark roux is the Creole tradition for gumbo and turtle soup, and New Orleans marchand de vin is often roux-bound too. How dark our own kitchen takes each one is a question for the chef.

At the table, a roux is part of why a gumbo or a turtle soup tastes deep rather than brothy. Questions about flour in a dish go to the kitchen.

The holy trinity is onion, celery and green bell pepper, chopped and softened together at the start of a Cajun or Creole dish. It is Louisiana's version of the French mirepoix, with bell pepper in place of carrot, which grew more easily in early Louisiana.

The name nods to the Catholic faith of the early settlers, and the phrase was most likely popularised by the chef Paul Prudhomme. Garlic is so often added that some cooks call it the pope.

The trinity is in our gumbo, the turtle soup, the Creole sauce on the Shrimp & Grits and the South Louisiana rice dressing. It is the reason those dishes taste of Louisiana before a single spice goes in.

Grits are dried corn ground coarse and simmered slowly in water or milk until creamy, the Southern answer to polenta. Stone-ground grits keep more of the corn's germ and flavour and take longer to cook than quick grits; hominy grits are made from corn treated with alkali.

They are a blank, comforting base that takes on butter, cheese and sauce.

We serve them two ways: Cheddar Grits as a breakfast side, and a fried pimento cheese grit cake, crisp outside and creamy inside, under the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits. Whether ours are stone-ground, and whose corn, are good questions for the kitchen.

Brown butter, beurre noisette in French, is butter cooked past melting until its milk solids toast to the colour of hazelnuts and it smells nutty and sweet. It must be stopped at that moment, often with lemon or vinegar, because a few seconds more and it burns bitter.

That nutty depth is why it appears across our menus in different forms.

On the Louisiana Crab Claws it becomes a warm brown butter vinaigrette, sharpened with acid; the spinach in the Turtle Soup is wilted in brown butter; and the financiers in the Blackberry Trifle are made with it, which is what makes them taste buttery rather than cakey.

The Baked Apple starts with a whole apple, peeled, cored and trimmed flat so it stands. A crumble of rolled oats, pecans, raisins, brown sugar and cinnamon is packed on top, and the apple bakes until a skewer slides through with no resistance. The brown sugar melts into the apple's juices and caramelises, which is where the glaze comes from.

It is the French baked apple meeting the British crumble, warm and soft under a little crunch.

It is the first plated course of the Traditional Breakfast, after the Brandy Milk Punch. Which apple the kitchen uses, and whether the tasting portion is whole or half, are good lineup questions.

Filet mignon is a small steak cut from the narrow end of the beef tenderloin, the muscle along the spine that does almost no work. That makes it the most tender cut on the animal and also one of the mildest, so it relies on its sauce and garnish for savour.

A petite filet is a small portion that cooks quickly: seared hard, finished gently and rested for a few minutes so the juices settle.

On the Traditional Breakfast it is the fourth course, with a crisp potato rösti, garlic spinach and a 4 oz pour of Côtes du Rhône. Take the guest's temperature when you take the tasting order, not when the course fires.

Garlic spinach is fresh spinach wilted quickly in a hot pan with oil or butter and sliced garlic, then squeezed of its water and seasoned at the last moment so it stays bright green rather than grey.

Rohan is not a breed but a proprietary cross created for D'Artagnan, a specialty meat company. It brings together the heritage Mallard and the Pekin, and the birds are raised for D'Artagnan on a farm in New York State's Catskills, without antibiotics, to about eleven weeks, longer than most commercial ducks.

We use it twice: the roasted breast on the dinner tasting and the confit leg on the Duck Confit Waffle. Say a special cross raised in New York, and do not call it a breed.

A duck breast carries a thick layer of fat under the skin, and the cook's job is to render most of it away while keeping the meat rosy. The skin is scored in a tight crosshatch, the breast goes skin-down into a cold or moderate pan, and the fat melts out slowly as the skin crisps. A short turn on the flesh side, a finish in the oven and a rest of a few minutes follow, then it is sliced across the grain.

Duck breast is served pink, like a steak; cooked through it turns grey and livery.

On the dinner tasting the Rohan breast comes with cane syrup-glazed peaches and candied hazelnuts. The usual doneness is medium-rare to medium; confirm at lineup.

Cane syrup is sugar cane juice boiled down in open kettles until thick, with nothing taken out. Molasses is what remains after sugar has been crystallised and removed, so cane syrup is sweeter, lighter and milder, with a buttery caramel taste rather than molasses's bitter edge. Steen's of Abbeville has made it since 1910, after a freeze threatened a cane crop.

It is a Louisiana pantry staple poured on biscuits, baked into cakes and used to glaze meat.

On the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast it glazes peaches, sweet and caramelised against rich duck. The menu does not name a brand, so say Louisiana cane syrup, a lighter cousin of molasses.

A trifle is an English layered pudding with centuries of history: sponge or biscuits soaked in sherry or juice, fruit, custard and whipped cream, built in a glass bowl so the layers show. It was a dish for gatherings and a way to use up cake.

A fruit curd is a cooked spread of fruit juice, sugar, egg yolks and butter, stirred over gentle heat until it thickens to coat a spoon, then chilled until set. Lemon curd is the British classic; blackberry curd uses the purée of the fruit, which gives a deep purple colour and a tart, jammy taste.

Curds are richer and sharper than jam and silkier than custard.

In the Blackberry Trifle the two curds are the bright, tart layers, purple and yellow, that keep the dessert from tasting sugary. They are made ahead and set cold, so the trifle can be built quickly to order. The service note lists what the curds contain.

A financier is a small French cake of ground almonds, egg whites, sugar, a little flour and brown butter, baked in a small mould. The standard account credits a Paris pâtissier named Lasne, whose shop stood near the stock exchange around 1890; he shaped them like little gold bars for the traders, and the name stuck.

In the Blackberry Trifle they are blackberry financier biscuits, the trifle's answer to sponge. The guide notes they are traditionally made with almond flour and asks you to confirm with the kitchen.

French toast is pain perdu, lost bread: stale bread rescued by soaking it in egg and milk, often with sugar and vanilla, and frying it in butter. In New Orleans it is an old Creole breakfast. The bread must be thick and slightly dry, or it soaks to mush; the pan must be moderate, so the custard centre sets before the outside burns.

Brioche makes the richest version, soft and custardy inside with a caramelised crust.

Our Framboise French Toast uses housemade citrus brioche, sold as a starter to share, and the children's breakfast offers a vanilla French toast with berries and whipped cream.

Café brûlot is New Orleans' flaming after-dinner coffee. Antoine's credits Jules Alciatore, the founder's son, with café brûlot diabolique in the late nineteenth century: brandy and orange liqueur flamed in a bowl with cinnamon, clove and a long spiral of orange and lemon peel, then ladled into strong coffee at the table. Brûlot comes from brûler, to burn.

It is one of the city's great tableside rituals.

Brennan's borrows its flavours for the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake: chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate cake, pecans, a spiced citrus glaze and whipped crème fraîche. The drink itself is not on our list, so sell the cake as the coffee's flavours, not the flame.

Grand Isle is the barrier island at the edge of the Louisiana coast. Grand Isle Jewels is a brand launched in April 2025 by JEDCO, the Jefferson Parish economic development commission, with the island's off-bottom oyster farmers.

Off-bottom farming raises oysters in cages that float or hang above the seafloor. The cages float just below the surface in an aquapark where ocean and estuary water mix, which keeps the oysters off the mud and gives them a briny, bright flavour, and the method is gentler on a storm-damaged coast than dredging wild reefs.

We serve them raw with a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette, at dinner and as the first course of the dinner tasting. Know the count per order, and ask the chef whether to tell the farming story.

On the Steak Tartare Cannoli it is grated over the top in place of the raw yolk of a classic tartare. It is the only dish on the current menus with it, so do not describe cured yolk as a standing house preparation.

The turtle in our soup is snapping turtle, a freshwater turtle. The wild alligator snapper has been off limits to commercial trappers in Louisiana since 2004, so restaurants buy it from licensed turtle farms, or buy common snapping turtle, which licensed collectors may still sell. The meat is dark, firm and rich, somewhere between veal and dark chicken, with plenty of gelatine, which gives the soup its body.

It is chopped finely and simmered for a long time, so it is tender and spread through the soup rather than served in chunks.

When a guest hesitates, describe the taste rather than the animal: rich, meaty and savoury, like a deep beef stew. The current supplier is a question for the chef, not a guess.

Canadian bacon is cured, lightly smoked pork loin, lean and ham-like, sliced into rounds; it is the meat of Eggs Benedict. A coffee cure rubs the loin with salt, sugar and ground coffee before it is smoked or roasted, adding a roasty, slightly bitter depth to the sweet, salty pork.

Our Sardou varies the house classic again: crispy artichokes, Parmesan creamed spinach, poached eggs and Choron sauce in place of hollandaise. Never present it as a Brennan's invention; it is Antoine's dish in the Brennan's style.

Eggs Owen shares its name with Owen Brennan, who founded the restaurant in 1946, and guests often guess it was named for him. The menu does not say so, and the restaurant has not published that story, so the guide's instruction stands: confirm at lineup before you tell it.

What can be said is how the plate relates to its neighbours. It takes the Hussarde's two sauces, hollandaise and marchand de vin, and replaces the Canadian bacon and muffin with red wine-braised short rib débris and a Creole-spiced potato, topped with a soft-boiled egg.

It is the heartier choice at $32 against the Hussarde at $27: steak and eggs, New Orleans style.

changes.before:
Braising cooks a tough, well-worked cut slowly in a little liquid in a covered pot, so its connective tissue melts into gelatin. Short rib is ideal: marbled, sinewy and full of flavour.

The ribs are seared hard for colour, the vegetables sweated, the pan deglazed with red wine and reduced, then stock added; the pot goes into a low oven for about three hours, until a fork turns the meat. The liquid is skimmed and reduced into a glossy sauce, and the meat is pulled back into it.

That is the short rib débris on the Eggs Owen: meltingly tender beef in a deep, winey gravy, which echoes the marchand de vin on the same plate.

An omelette is beaten eggs cooked quickly in a hot buttered pan. The French omelette is stirred as it sets, then rolled into a smooth, pale cylinder with a soft, creamy centre and barely any colour. The American omelette is set flat, filled, and folded in half, firmer and lightly golden.

Either way the filling goes in warm, so the eggs are not overcooked waiting for it.

Our Crab & Corn Omelette is filled with Louisiana lump crab and roasted sweet corn, with miso butter, lemon, basil and a Marcona almond gremolata. Which style the kitchen makes is a fair question to ask at lineup, so you can describe it before it lands.

The hanger steak, onglet in France, hangs from the diaphragm near the kidneys. There is only one per animal, which is why butchers used to keep it for themselves and why it was long called the butcher's steak. A tough sinew runs down its centre and is cut out, leaving two loose-grained lobes.

It is intensely beefy and best cooked hot and fast to medium-rare or medium, rested, and sliced across the grain; past medium it tightens and tastes of liver.

We serve two: the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak at breakfast and lunch with béarnaise and an egg, and the Creole Hanger Steak at dinner with chilli crisp. Always take the temperature.

For a fish fillet, the pan and fat are hot before it goes in, often skin or presentation side first; it is left alone to colour, then turned once and finished gently so it stays moist and flakes at the touch. Thin, delicate fish cook in two or three minutes; thicker fillets are finished in the oven.

The children's Sautéed Gulf Fish is cooked this way, and the Pecan Gulf Fish is likely pan-roasted or sautéed to order. Know today's fish and its preparation at lineup.

Flambé means flamed: spirit added to a hot pan and lit, so the alcohol vapour burns in a burst of blue and orange flame. It is theatre and flavour at once, caramelising the sauce's surface. At Brennan's it is done on a guéridon, the tableside cart.

The guide's steps are learned word for word: measure the spirit into a small vessel, never pour from the bottle near a flame, pull the pan off the flame to add it, tilt to ignite, keep a lid in reach, let the flame die before plating, and turn the burner off before leaving.

In a bright breakfast room the flame can be almost invisible, so treat the pan as lit until it clearly has died down.

The Ursuline nuns, who came to New Orleans in 1727, are credited by tradition with bringing the recipe; Louisiana cooks swapped in pecans and made a soft, creamy patty of brown sugar, butter and cream.

In the nineteenth century pralinières, women street vendors, many of them free women of color, sold them in the French Quarter.

On the New Orleans Bread Pudding pralines add crunch and caramel sweetness. Say PRAH-leen; PRAY-leen marks a visitor.

A Bavarian cream, bavarois in French, is a crème anglaise set with gelatin and lightened with whipped cream, then chilled in a mould. It sits between a mousse and a custard: light, silky and holding its shape. The great nineteenth-century chef Carême codified it.

Chocolate melted into the custard turns it into a chocolate Bavarian.

The Snickers's Bavarian milk chocolate almost certainly means a milk chocolate bavarois, not chocolate from Bavaria. The guide notes Bavarian creams are usually set with gelatin, so check with the kitchen for guests who avoid it.

A caramel custard is eggs, milk or cream and sugar cooked gently until set, flavoured with caramel, sugar cooked to amber, which brings a toasty, slightly bitter depth. It is the family of crème caramel and flan.

Gentle heat is everything: too hot and the eggs curdle into a grainy, weeping custard.

In The Snickers it plays the caramel layer of the candy bar, silky and toasty against the milk chocolate Bavarian cream, the nougat ice cream and the salty roasted peanuts. If a guest asks, it is the soft caramel part of the bar.

The French tarte au citron is sweet pastry filled with a sharp lemon curd, often crowned with meringue. Our Lemon Tart takes it apart: the pastry becomes a sweet pastry crumb, the curd becomes a light yuzu mousse, the sharpness is concentrated in a lemon jelly, and the meringue is piped and toasted.

The deconstruction keeps the flavours and makes the whole dessert lighter.

It is $14 and the lightest dessert on the list. The guide names it, with the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, as the dessert to steer to for guests who avoid alcohol, since the flamed desserts and the bread pudding all carry spirits.

Tarte Tatin is the French upside-down tart: fruit caramelised in butter and sugar in a pan, covered with pastry, baked and turned out so the pastry is underneath. It is named for Stéphanie and Caroline Tatin, who ran the Hôtel Tatin at Lamotte-Beuvron in the Sologne. Pineapple is a tropical fruit, sweet and sharp, and much juicier than apple. Charring it, in a very hot pan, under a grill or in caramel, drives off water and caramelises its sugars until the edges blacken slightly, giving a deep, almost smoky sweetness while keeping the acidity.

That browning is what makes it work in a tart built for apples.

Cheddar takes its name from the English village of Cheddar, and is now made all over the world. Sharp cheddar melts well and holds its flavour in a sauce.

Montreal seasoning is the steak spice of Montreal's smoked meat delis. Ours is the five the sheet prints: black pepper, caraway, coriander, chili flake and mustard seed, so it is peppery and aromatic, with its heat from the chili flake. A shop-bought blend may list other things; say only our five.

Caraway matters here. Its anise-like seed is what gives many rye breads their familiar flavour, so the seasoning and the rye tuile echo each other across the plate.

The deli story is real as far as it goes: Schwartz's, the Montreal smoked meat house, dates from 1928 and had a Romanian-Jewish founder. The tale that the spice began with a lunch at a deli in the 1940s is not verified, so tell it as a tale and give it no date. How much heat tonight's blend carries is the chef's answer.

Its flesh is firm and dense with a mildly sweet flavour, and it is cut into thick steaks or fillets rather than thin ones, which is why it is cooked more like a piece of meat than a delicate fish: a hard sear or a grill, then a gentle finish, and it dries out if it is taken too far.

Chateaubriand, shah-toh-bree-AHN, is the name butchers now use for the thick centre cut of the beef tenderloin, the muscle along the spine that does almost no work. That is why it is the most tender cut on the animal, and also why it is comparatively lean: tenderness and heavy marbling are different qualities, and a tenderloin has the first without much of the second. Braising is slow, covered cooking in a little liquid, and greens take to it the way a tough cut of meat does. Collards are a sturdy leaf of the cabbage family with a stem and a rib that stay chewy if they are only wilted, so Southern kitchens cook them long and low in a flavoured liquid, often with smoked pork, until the leaves turn silky and sweet and the bitterness softens. The liquid they cook in, the pot liquor, becomes a seasoning in its own right.

On the Agnolotti del Plin the braised collards are the Southern voice beside a Piedmontese pasta, soft and earthy against the pork, the ricotta and the Parmesan. The sheet does not print what ours braise in, and it marks Alcohol for the plate without saying where, so do not describe a ham hock or a splash of wine: say slow-cooked greens and learn the braise at lineup.

The shank is the lower leg of the lamb, a hard-working muscle wrapped in connective tissue and set around a bone. It is the opposite of a loin chop: cooked fast it stays tough, cooked slowly in liquid it turns tender and deeply flavoured, because hours of gentle, moist heat melt that sinew into gelatin and the meat gives up its grip on the bone.

That is why our kitchen cooks it as a daube, DOHB, the slow braise of Provence, before it goes into the pastry. The braise does the tenderising; the oven only has to crisp the crust.

The sheet does not say whether the bone comes to the table inside the pastry, whether the meat is boned and formed, or what the portion is. Learn the build at lineup and describe the lamb as tender and slow-cooked, which is the one thing the cut promises.

Jus, ZHOO, is French for juice, and in a kitchen it means the natural cooking juices of a roast or a braise, strained and reduced into a thin, glossy sauce that tastes of the meat itself rather than of flour or cream. A lamb jus is built on lamb bones and trimmings, and it is the lightest, purest sauce a lamb can have.

Ours is spiced: the sheet names star anise, orange and a touch of cinnamon. Those are warm, aromatic flavours, the scent of a winter kitchen, and there is no chilli in the list, so a guest who asks whether it is spicy should hear warm, not hot.

What else goes into it, which stock, any wine, how far it is reduced and whether it is finished with butter, is not printed. Describe the three aromatics with confidence and send the rest to the kitchen.

Star anise is the dried, star-shaped fruit of an evergreen tree native to south China and Vietnam, each point of the star holding one shiny seed. It tastes of liquorice, sweet, warm and a little peppery, the same note you know from the Herbsaint in a Sazerac, though the two come from different plants, and it is the flavour that anchors Chinese five-spice.

In a braise or a sauce it is used whole and sparingly, one or two stars steeped in the liquid and lifted out, because it is strong enough to take over a pot. With orange and cinnamon, as in our spiced lamb jus, it makes a warm, aromatic sauce that smells of fall rather than of heat.

The sheet names it, with orange and a touch of cinnamon, as the scent of the jus; how much goes in and what else joins it is the kitchen's business.

Daube, DOHB, is the slow-cooked meat dish of Provence: pieces of meat cooked for hours in wine with aromatic vegetables and herbs, covered and at a bare simmer, until they are tender enough to cut with a spoon. It is a dish for a tough cut and a cold evening. Beef is the best known, but Marseille's own account of the dish names lamb among the meats it can be made with, and the recipe changes from one kitchen to the next.

The method is braising: sear for colour, add the liquid and aromatics, then low heat and patience, so the tough cut's connective tissue melts into gelatin and the liquid becomes the sauce.

Our lamb shank daube goes into puff pastry afterwards. What it is braised in, which aromatics go in and whether wine stays in the finished dish are not printed; send that to the kitchen rather than guess.

A terrine takes its name from the deep earthenware mould it is cooked in: a filling is packed into the mould, cooked gently, often in a water bath, then cooled, turned out and sliced. Most people know the pork and liver terrine of a French charcuterie counter; a fish terrine works the same way, with fish in place of the meat, and comes out firm enough to slice cleanly and delicate to eat.

Stuffed means there is a filling at the centre, so a slice shows one thing wrapped in another: a layer of fish around a softer or differently coloured centre.

On the Fish Bouillabaisse the terrine is the fish of the dish. The sheet does not name the fish, what fills it or whether the slice comes warm or cold, so claim none of it; learn the build at lineup and describe the slice with confidence once you have seen it.

A shrimp mousse is raw shrimp puréed to a smooth paste, seasoned and lightened, then cooked gently so it sets soft and pale, like a savoury custard that tastes of sweet shrimp. In the classic French kitchen the paste is bound with egg white and enriched with cream, pressed through a sieve and poached or baked in a water bath; it is the same idea as a quenelle, the poached dumpling of fish or shellfish.

The point is texture: a mousse is airy and tender where a whole shrimp is firm, so it melts against the terrine and the sauce.

On the Fish Bouillabaisse it brings the shellfish side of a bouillabaisse to a plate that has no shells on it, and the sheet marks Dairy, Eggs and Shellfish for the plate without saying where each sits, so what binds and enriches tonight's mousse is the kitchen's answer. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

Aioli, eye-OH-lee, is the garlic sauce of Provence, and the word says so: ai is garlic and oli is oil in Provençal. Garlic is pounded to a paste with salt and olive oil is worked in drop by drop until the sauce is thick and glossy; most kitchens add egg yolk to hold it, which makes it a garlic mayonnaise. It is the sauce of the grand aïoli, the Provençal platter of fish and vegetables.

Ours is flavoured with preserved lemon, lemon cured in salt and its own juice for weeks until the rind turns soft, salty and perfumed rather than sour; we use it in the beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique and on the Smoked Cauliflower.

On the Marseille table the sauce beside a bouillabaisse is rouille, a rust-coloured garlic sauce with red pepper. The sheet names an aioli, not rouille, so say aioli. What is in tonight's batch is the kitchen's answer.

Bouillabaisse, boo-yuh-BESS, is the fish soup of Marseille, and in the city it comes in two parts: a broth, and the fish that cooked in it, served apart. The broth gives the dish its name and its character, and the usual make is fish simmered with olive oil, onion, garlic, fennel and tomato, boiled hard so the oil and the broth come together, then strained; saffron and pastis are usual, and rouille, a rust-coloured garlic sauce, is spread on croutons beside it.

A bouillabaisse sauce is that broth taken further, usually reduced so it coats a spoon and dresses the terrine and the mousse rather than filling a bowl. The flavours of the soup arrive as a sauce.

The sheet prints the name and no recipe. Whether ours carries saffron, tomato, fennel or pastis, and what the Alcohol and Nightshades marks point to, are the chef's answers; say the Marseille broth made into a sauce, and no more.

Burnt means the cut face is charred, under a torch, a salamander or in a very hot pan, until the sugars on the surface caramelise and darken. Aguachile, ah-gwah-CHEE-leh, means chilli water. It is the raw seafood preparation of Sinaloa on Mexico's Pacific coast: in its classic form, raw shrimp are covered in lime juice blended with fresh chilli, with onion and cucumber, and eaten at once, before the acid has done more than brighten them. It is a cousin of ceviche, but faster and hotter, a sauce poured over rather than a cure.

Ours is the kitchen's own version for tuna: carrot for sweetness and colour, ginger for a clean warmth, with chilli for heat. The sheet names the sauce and nothing of its build: not the acid, the chilli, the proportions or how hot the finished batch is, and the classic recipe's lime, shrimp and cucumber are not promised on our plate.

Describe it as a sweet, warm, chilli-bright sauce over raw tuna, and confirm the heat with the kitchen before you call it mild.

Maldon salt is a flake sea salt made on the Essex coast of England, where seawater is drawn in and evaporated gently until the salt crystallises at the surface in hollow pyramids. Those pyramid-shaped flakes are the whole point: they are crisp and light, they dissolve quickly on the tongue, and a pinch gives a clean burst of salt with none of the harshness of a fine-ground salt.

It is a finishing salt, pinched over at the end rather than cooked in, and on the Chocolate Crémeux it does what salt always does to chocolate: it makes the chocolate taste more of itself and seems to make it sweeter, without adding sugar, while the crisp flakes add a second crunch beside the nibs. The sheet names it on the Tuna Crudo of the same tasting as well. Say the name as the sheet prints it, Maldon, and let the guest taste the flake.

Seawater is drawn from the coast, filtered and evaporated slowly in open pans until the salt crystallises at the surface into hollow, pyramid-shaped flakes, which are raked out and dried; the pyramid is the shape the maker is known by. The flakes are crisp and light, dissolve quickly and give a clean salt taste, which is why kitchens keep a box at the pass to finish a plate rather than to season a pot.

At Brennan's the name is printed twice on the Fall 2026 sheets: as the finishing salt on the Chocolate Crémeux and on the Tuna Crudo, both courses of the Fall tasting menu.

Pepper is the dried fruit of Piper nigrum, a climbing vine of the Malabar Coast of Kerala in south-western India, where it has been grown and traded for thousands of years. Green peppercorns are the unripe berries, black ones the unripe berries dried until the skin wrinkles and darkens, and white ones the ripe berries with the skin soaked off, so the three are one plant at different stages.

Tellicherry is a grade of large peppercorn left longer on the vine, named for the port the British shipped pepper from in the 1600s, now called Thalassery. The trade has moved: by the International Pepper Community's count Vietnam grew 43 per cent of the world's 561,500 tonnes in 2020, the most of any country, with Brazil, Indonesia, India and Sri Lanka behind it.

Cooks buy pepper whole and crack or grind it to order, because its aroma fades within hours of grinding. The menus print no grade or supplier; the pepper behind the barbecue sauce and the mignonette is a question for the chef.

Chocolate is made from the fermented, roasted seeds of the cacao tree, which is native to the upper Amazon; the oldest trace of its use, about 5,300 years old, was found in Ecuador. Ground, the seeds become chocolate liquor, and its share sets the style. In the United States a bittersweet or semisweet bar holds at least 35 per cent chocolate liquor, and pastry cooks usually mean 60 to 72 per cent cacao: dark, with enough sugar to bake. Milk chocolate holds at least 10 per cent liquor and 12 per cent milk solids, sweeter and softer.

The Café Brûlot Coffee Cake bakes bittersweet chocolate with chicory coffee, which deepens it, since coffee and chocolate share roasted, bitter notes. The Snickers' Bavarian milk chocolate is read as milk chocolate in a Bavarian cream, not chocolate from Bavaria. No maker is printed: a question for the chef. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

A glaze on a cake is sugar dissolved in a little liquid and set thin over the top: icing sugar beaten with citrus juice, or a syrup of sugar, juice and zest boiled briefly and brushed over the warm cake so it soaks in and dries to a sheen. It adds sweetness and shine, and here it carries the flavours the cake is named for.

Café brûlot, the New Orleans coffee flamed at the table, is made with orange and lemon peel, cinnamon and clove, and the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake borrows those: the glaze is where the citrus and the warm spice live, over the chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate cake, with pecans for crunch and whipped crème fraîche to cut the sweetness. The menu prints only spiced citrus glaze. Which citrus, which spices, and whether any brandy goes into it, as it does into the drink, are questions for the chef.

An heirloom tomato is an open-pollinated variety whose saved seed grows true, year after year, unlike a hybrid, whose seed is made by crossing two parents each season. How old a variety must be is not agreed, fifty years by one rule, a hundred by another. Heirlooms are grown for flavour and colour, not for shipping: thin skins, odd shapes, red, pink, yellow, green and near-black, like the dusky Cherokee Purple or the big pink Brandywine. They crack and bruise, so they are sold close to home.

On the Creole Tomato Tostada they are mixed with Creole tomatoes, Louisiana's summer tomato, and served raw with burrata, the okra tostada and smoked tomato water. The menu prints Louisiana heirloom, so the fruit is local; which farm grows it is a question for the chef, and the dish goes when the tomatoes do.

Worcestershire sauce is a thin, dark, fermented seasoning first sold in 1837 by two chemists in Worcester, England, Lea & Perrins, and the firm still makes it there. The bottle lists vinegar, molasses, sugar, salt, anchovies, tamarind, onion, garlic and spices, so it is salty, sour, sweet and deeply savoury at once, and because of the anchovies it is a fish product for a guest who asks. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

It is the savoury backbone of New Orleans barbecue shrimp, the pan sauce of butter, black pepper, Worcestershire, garlic and lemon born at Pascal's Manale in 1954, the style the guide gives for the barbecue sauce on the Louisiana Oysters and the Louisiana BBQ Lobster. A classic Caesar dressing carries it too, though ours is a smoked oyster dressing. Whether our barbecue sauce and that dressing use it, and which brand, are questions for the chef.

Worcestershire sauce began with two chemists of Broad Street, Worcester, John Wheeley Lea and William Henry Perrins, partners from 1823. The company's story says a governor of Bengal, Lord Sandys, brought a recipe home from India and asked them to make it up, and that the first batch was so harsh it was left in casks and forgotten until it had mellowed; the firm itself allows that the recipe's origin is unclear, and the story is tradition rather than record. The sauce went on sale in 1837, by some accounts reaching the public in 1838 once the casks had matured.

It has been made in a factory on Midland Road in Worcester since 1897. The company passed to HP Foods in 1930 and, with HP, to Heinz in 2005. The British bottle lists malt vinegar, spirit vinegar, molasses, sugar, salt, anchovies, tamarind extract, onion, garlic, spices and flavourings; the American bottle is built on distilled white vinegar and molasses and lists anchovies too.

In New Orleans it is the savoury depth of barbecue shrimp, the Pascal's Manale pan sauce of 1954, and so of the barbecue sauce on our Louisiana Oysters and BBQ Lobster. The menus print no brand, and whether the house sauce uses it at all is the chef's to confirm.

Whipping beats air into fat. As cold cream is whisked, its fat globules partly join and trap the bubbles, so the cream thickens to soft peaks, then firm; a minute more and it turns grainy and then to butter. Cream needs about 30 per cent fat to hold air, and United States heavy cream is at least 36 per cent, which is what a kitchen whips. Everything must be cold, the cream and the bowl.

The same technique lightens richer creams. The Framboise French Toast prints a mascarpone mousse, the rich Italian fresh cheese whipped light with cream; the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake prints whipped crème fraîche, whose tang keeps the cake from being too sweet; the Pineapple Tarte Tatin prints a whipped vanilla mousse, the Snickers' Bavarian cream is lightened with whipped cream, and the children's Vanilla French Toast prints whipped cream plainly. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

Butter is cream churned until its fat gathers and the buttermilk runs off: about eighty per cent milk fat, with water and milk solids. The solids are what brown in a beurre noisette and what burn, so a kitchen clarifies butter, melting it and lifting off the clear fat, for hollandaise and for sautéing fish at a high heat. Cold butter whisked into a reduction makes a beurre blanc; soft butter beaten with foie gras or miso makes a compound butter.

Butter is in nearly every savoury plate we serve. It is the body of the hollandaise, béarnaise, Choron and Foyot, the beurre blanc on the redfish, the brown butter on the crab claws and in the turtle soup, the New Orleans BBQ sauce, the garlic butter finish on the Brabant potatoes, and the pan the Bananas Foster begins in.

Whose butter the kitchen buys is not printed. Questions about dairy go to the service note and the kitchen.

The shallot is a small, copper-skinned member of the onion family, growing in clusters like garlic, with a finer, sweeter flavour than an onion and none of its harshness once cooked. Minced, it dissolves into a sauce; sliced raw, it keeps a gentle bite.

French sauce cooking begins with it. Béarnaise, and so the Choron on the Sardou and the Foyot on the Chateaubriand, starts with shallot reduced in vinegar with tarragon; a beurre blanc starts the same way with white wine; a mignonette is raw shallot in vinegar; a mustard cream sauce sweats it in butter. Brennan's own published marchand de vin sweats onion, shallot and garlic together, though tonight's build is the chef's to confirm.

The menu prints shallots twice, on the Louisiana Oysters and beside the turnips of the Poussin à la Moutarde. Everywhere else they are inside the sauce, and a guest who asks about onions should hear so.

Parsley is the kitchen's green workhorse, the flat-leaf kind in most restaurant kitchens because its flavour is cleaner and stronger than the curly sort. Chopped fine at the last moment it tastes fresh, grassy and faintly peppery; cooked long it fades to almost nothing, which is why it goes on at the end.

It is one of the four fines herbes on the crab claws, half of the persillade on the dinner hanger with garlic and pepitas, the classic green in a gremolata with lemon zest, and the finish of the Brabant potatoes with garlic butter. A New Orleans bordelaise, the family the pecan sauce most likely belongs to, is butter, garlic and parsley. The Grand Isle Jewel oysters print it plainly beside the mignonette.

Which herbs go into tonight's gremolata on the omelette is the chef's answer; say herbs, citrus and almonds until you know.

Red wine in a pan does three things: its acid brightens, its tannin and colour deepen a sauce, and as it reduces its fruit concentrates into something savoury and winey. Boiling drives off most of the alcohol but never all of it, and a sauce reduced by half carries the wine's character strongly, so a thin, sharp wine makes a thin, sharp sauce.

Two of our plates are built on it. The marchand de vin, the wine merchant's sauce under the eggs on the Hussarde and the Owen, is red wine cooked with aromatics and beef stock into a glossy brown sauce. The short rib on the Eggs Owen is braised in red wine for hours, and the braising liquid, skimmed and reduced, becomes the gravy the débris falls into.

Which wine the kitchen cooks with is not printed. A guest who avoids alcohol should know both plates carry it, as the service note says.

Wilted with garlic beside the Petite Filet Mignon, it stays light and green. Wilted in brown butter and folded through the Turtle Soup, it turns nutty.

Whether the side and the Sardou's spinach are one preparation, and whether either carries stock, is confirmed with the kitchen for a guest who asks about meat. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

Dijon has been France's mustard town for centuries, and the modern style dates from 1856, when Jean Naigeon of Dijon replaced the vinegar in his mustard with verjuice, the sour juice of unripe grapes. Today's Dijon is brown mustard seed ground with white wine, vinegar, water and salt in place of that verjuice: smooth, pale and sharp.

The name is not protected. A 1937 decree defined Dijon mustard by its method, not its town, so the name is generic: it can be made anywhere. France needs about 35,000 tonnes of seed a year and buys about 80 per cent of it from Canada, from the prairies of Alberta and Saskatchewan; when drought there halved the crop in 2021, French shelves ran short of Dijon in 2022. The protected name is Moutarde de Bourgogne, an IGP registered in 2009, which must be made with seed grown in Burgundy and Bourgogne white wine; Edmond Fallot of Beaune makes one with Bourgogne Aligoté. The best-known old name is Maille, founded in Paris in 1747 by Antoine-Claude Maille, a supplier to the court of Louis XV, which Maurice Grey of Grey Poupon bought in 1885.

Brennan's prints mustard twice, in the mustard maple syrup on the Duck Confit Waffle and the mustard cream sauce on the Poussin à la Moutarde, and names no kind or maker. The guide calls Burgundy Dijon mustard's home when it pairs the poussin with a Mâcon, a fair line for the table, but not a claim that the kitchen's mustard is Dijon.
changes.after:
Dijon has been France's mustard town for centuries, and the modern style dates from 1856, when Jean Naigeon of Dijon replaced the vinegar in his mustard with verjuice, the sour juice of unripe grapes. Today's Dijon is brown mustard seed ground with white wine, vinegar, water and salt in place of that verjuice: smooth, pale and sharp.

The name is not protected. A 1937 decree defined Dijon mustard by its method, not its town, so the name is generic: it can be made anywhere. France needs about 35,000 tonnes of seed a year and buys about 80 percent of it from Canada, from the prairies of Alberta and Saskatchewan; when drought there halved the crop in 2021, French shelves ran short of Dijon in 2022. The protected name is Moutarde de Bourgogne, an IGP registered in 2009, which must be made with seed grown in Burgundy and Bourgogne white wine; Edmond Fallot of Beaune makes one with Bourgogne Aligoté. The best-known old name is Maille, founded in Paris in 1747 by Antoine-Claude Maille, a supplier to the court of Louis XV, which Maurice Gray of Gray Poupon bought in 1885.

Brennan's prints mustard twice, in the mustard maple syrup on the Duck Confit Waffle and the mustard cream sauce on the Poussin à la Moutarde, and names no kind or maker. The guide calls Burgundy Dijon mustard's home when it pairs the poussin with a Mâcon, a fair line for the table, but not a claim that the kitchen's mustard is Dijon.

A compound butter is soft butter beaten with something that flavours it, then chilled so a slice or a spoonful can be dropped onto hot food and melt into a sauce on the plate. The French classic is maître d'hôtel butter, with parsley and lemon, for a grilled steak; a kitchen can beat in herbs, garlic, anchovy, miso, foie gras or toasted nuts.

The plate's own heat finishes it.

Two of our plates print one. The foie gras butter on the Duck Confit Waffle is fattened liver puréed into butter, melting into the waffle's pockets with the mustard maple syrup. The house-made miso butter on the Crab & Corn Omelette is the fermented paste beaten into butter, salty and savoury against the sweet crab and corn. The pecan bordelaise on the Gulf fish, if it is the New Orleans garlic butter the guide says to confirm, is a close cousin with toasted pecans worked in.

Stock is water in which bones and aromatics have simmered for hours, strained and skimmed: the savoury liquid most sauces, soups and braises are built on. Brown stock, from roasted bones, is deep and gelatinous; chicken and fish stocks are lighter. Reduced hard, brown stock becomes glace de viande, GLAHS duh vee-AHND, a syrup that sets firm when cold and deepens any sauce.

Escoffier built his sauce families on stock, and our brown sauces do: the marchand de vin under the Hussarde and the Owen is red wine and beef stock, the short rib braise is wine and stock, and sauce Foyot on the Chateaubriand is béarnaise with meat glaze whisked in. Stock also underlies the gumbo, the turtle soup, the Creole sauce, the braised leeks and, likely, the lobster's white bean stew.

Which stocks the kitchen keeps, and whether a vegetable plate touches one, is the chef's answer. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

Roselle, Hibiscus sabdariffa, is the hibiscus of food and drink: a tall annual whose fleshy red calyces, the cups around each seed pod, are picked and dried. Where it began is argued. Some favour Sudan, where it may have been domesticated about 6,000 years ago, others West Africa, others the stretch from India to Malaysia; there is a fibre strain and a food strain, and the food strain is the one in the kitchen.

The trade today is spread across three continents. China, Sudan and Thailand are the major growers; Sudanese roselle is held to be the finest, but an American trade embargo and large scale planting in Mexico, Thailand and China moved the market, and Mexico's own crop grew by more than half between 2009 and 2019. Every culture that grows it drinks it: agua de Jamaica in Mexico, the dried calyces boiled eight to ten minutes and sweetened; bissap in West Africa; karkadé in Egypt.

The calyx is tart with fruit acids and deep red with the same family of pigments as a red grape skin, so a pickling liquid made with it colours whatever sits in it. On the Redfish Véronique that is the grapes. The menu prints hibiscus and nothing more: whether the kitchen uses whole dried calyces or a brewed tea, and whose, is not public.

A table grape is a grape bred to be eaten, not pressed: thin skinned, crisp, juicy and usually seedless, sweeter to bite than a wine grape and lower in sugar. In the United States nearly all of them, about 99 per cent, grow in California, which is where a grape on an American plate most likely began unless the menu says otherwise.

The French classic behind our Redfish Véronique calls for peeled muscat grapes warmed in the sauce. Ours are a modern turn on that: grapes pickled in a hibiscus brine, so they keep their crunch and sweetness under a red, tart skin, and eat more like a relish than a fruit. The variety and the grower are not printed, so say grapes, pickled with hibiscus, and let the chef name the rest.

Sweet tea is the house drink of the American South: black tea brewed strong, sugared while it is hot so the sugar dissolves, then poured over ice. The oldest printed recipe is in a Virginia cookbook of 1879, made then with green tea; black tea took over, and the first printed black tea version is said to be a Boston cookbook of 1884. Tea itself is the leaf of Camellia sinensis, black tea the fully oxidised leaf, and nearly all of it is imported; the one large tea farm in the country is on Wadmalaw Island near Charleston.

In the kitchen it is a brine. The Poussin à la Moutarde is a Cornish hen soaked in sweet tea with salt before it is fried: the salt seasons the bird and keeps it juicy, the tea's tannin and the sugar help the skin brown deep. Which tea, how sweet and how long are the chef's details.

Cold tea in America began as punch: the oldest printed recipes are green tea punches with spirits or wine, such as the tea punch in The Kentucky Housewife of 1839. The oldest printed sweet tea is in Housekeeping in Old Virginia, a Virginia community cookbook of 1879: green tea steeped, two teaspoons to a quart, poured over ice with sugar in each goblet and a squeeze of lemon suggested. Mrs Lincoln's Boston Cook Book of 1884 is cited as the first printed iced tea made with black tea, and black tea is what the South drinks now, brewed strong and sweetened while hot.

Tea is the leaf of Camellia sinensis; black tea is the leaf fully oxidised before it is dried. Almost all tea drunk in the United States is imported. The one large scale tea farm in the country is the Charleston Tea Garden on Wadmalaw Island, South Carolina, 127 acres with about 40 under tea, whose bushes descend from plants the French botanist André Michaux brought to the Carolinas in the late 1700s; smaller farms work in Alabama, Hawaii, Oregon and Washington.

On the dinner menu sweet tea is a brine: the Poussin à la Moutarde is a Cornish hen soaked in sweet tea with salt before frying, the Southern fried chicken way. The menu names the brine and nothing else. Which tea is brewed, how much sugar and salt go in, whether the tea is made in house and how long the bird sits are open questions for the chef.

Paprika and cayenne are the same plant at two ends of a scale: Capsicum annuum, the pepper Columbus carried home from the Americas around 1493. Paprika is the sweet or mildly hot pod dried and ground fine: it reached Hungary under Ottoman rule in the 16th century and by the 19th was the national spice, grown around Szeged and Kalocsa; Spain's pimentón de la Vera is dried over oak smoke. It gives colour, sweetness and a gentle warmth, and it scorches easily, so it goes into a rub or in late. Cayenne is a thin hot pod ground whole, named by a folk association with the town in French Guiana, and used by the pinch.

Together they are the red in every Louisiana blend: the classic blackening mix is paprika led with cayenne, and Creole seasoning is built on both. What the house blend holds, and how hot the tofu's crust is, is the kitchen's to say.

A steak's temperature is the first thing a server writes on the ticket. Rare is a cool red centre; medium-rare a warm red centre, about 130 to 135°F inside; medium pink and warm; medium-well a trace of pink; well done cooked through and grey. The federal guidance for a whole cut of beef is 145°F with a three minute rest, and cooking below that, as most steak houses do, is a stated preference. A cook pulls the meat early because it keeps cooking as it rests, rising 5 to 15°F.

Our hangers are at their best medium-rare to medium: past medium the loose grain tightens and tastes of liver. The Chateaubriand serves two, so ask the temperature once for the table, and the Petite Filet's temperature is taken with the tasting order, not when the course fires. Take it as you take the order, repeat it back, and write it down.

Two habits make a steak eat well after it leaves the heat. The first is the rest: a few minutes on a board before it is cut, during which the centre keeps cooking by 5 to 15°F, so the cook pulls it early and lets the rest finish it. The old story that the juices soak back into the fibres is contested; what is sure is that meat cut while it is hottest bleeds the most, so a short rest keeps the plate dry and the slice juicy.

The second is the knife. Muscle fibres run in one direction, and a slice cut across them leaves short fibres that part easily, where a slice along them chews like rope. The hanger's loose grain is sliced across after its rest, a Chateaubriand is rested about ten minutes and carved thick across the grain, and the duck breast on the tasting is sliced the same way.

Roasting a joint whole, rather than cutting it into steaks first, keeps the centre moist and evenly rosy while the outside browns. A Chateaubriand is roasted at a moderate heat until its centre reads about medium-rare, then rested about ten minutes and carved in thick slices across the grain, so every slice has a crust and a pink heart. Ours is roasted whole for two, and one temperature serves the whole roast, which is why the guide says to ask once for the table.

It takes longer than a single steak: confirm the timing with the kitchen and set it before the order, so the table is not waiting in silence. Carving at the table belongs to the guéridon tradition the house keeps for its flamed desserts; whether tonight's roast is carved at the table or in the kitchen is confirmed at lineup, so ask before you promise it.

A glaze is a shine that tastes of something. For a vegetable it is a French classic: the pieces are cooked in a shallow pan with a little water, butter, salt and often a pinch of sugar, under a paper lid, until the liquid cooks away and what is left coats each piece in a sweet, savoury gloss; Escoffier's Vichy carrots of 1903 are the model, and glazed turnips are made the same way. For a roast or a fruit the glaze is a syrup, a reduced stock or a reduced wine brushed on and set under heat until it clings.

The menu prints glazed four times: the summer squash beside the Chateaubriand, the Madeira-glazed broccolini on the Creole Hanger Steak, the cane syrup-glazed peaches with the Rohan duck and the Succotash's summer vegetables. Beyond the Madeira and the cane syrup it names, what each glaze is made of is a question for the chef.

Searing is the hard, hot start that gives meat its crust. The surface is patted dry, because water holds a pan at the boil and nothing browns until it has gone, then laid in a smoking pan and left alone until it releases. The brown is the Maillard reaction, my-YAR, named for the French chemist who described it in 1912: at roughly 140 to 165 C the meat's amino acids and sugars react into hundreds of new flavour compounds and the dark pigments of a crust. It does not seal in juices, an old story, but it is where most of a steak's savour comes from.

Our hangers are cooked hot and fast, the Petite Filet is seared hard and finished gently, the Owen's short rib is seared before it braises, a roast like the Chateaubriand is usually seared first, and blackening is searing taken to its edge, a spice crust set in seconds on the Blackened Tofu.

USDA grades are a quality stamp, not a cut. A federal grader scores a carcass on marbling, the flecks of fat within the muscle, and on maturity, the animal's age, and the packer pays for the service by choice. Prime is the most marbled beef from young cattle, Choice the broad middle with small to moderate marbling, Select the leanest. Prime was scarce for decades, a few per cent of graded beef; the USDA's own grading reports put it near 10 per cent in 2024 and 2025, and weekly counts since have run higher as marbling has climbed.

Marbling melts as the steak cooks, basting the muscle from inside, so a Prime steak eats richer and more tender. Brennan's prints Prime once, on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak; Creekstone grades Prime and Choice, so say Prime only where the menu does, and never promote the dinner hanger or the Chateaubriand unless the kitchen confirms it.

Corn, maize to most of the world, was domesticated in the Balsas valley of southern Mexico about nine thousand years ago and is the grain of the Americas. It reaches a kitchen in several forms. Sweet corn is picked young, while the kernels are full of sugar and milky juice, and eaten as a vegetable. Field corn, the dent kinds, is left to dry hard and ground: coarse for grits, finer for cornmeal and cornbread. Hominy is dried corn soaked in an alkali, which loosens the hull and changes the flavour.

On our menus corn is the Cheddar Grits and the fried pimento cheese grit cake under the Shrimp & Grits, the cornmeal in the cornbread and chive waffle, and the roasted sweet corn in the Crab & Corn Omelette.

Whether tonight's Succotash carries corn, as the traditional dish does, is learned at lineup; so is whose corn the grits are ground from.

Rice is Louisiana's grain. It is grown on the prairie of the southwest, where planting began in earnest in the early 1880s and the 1890 crop made Louisiana the leading rice state; Crowley, in Acadia Parish, became the centre of the industry and the home of the LSU rice station from 1909. Long grain is the Louisiana habit: grains that cook separate and firm rather than clinging, the right thing under a gumbo or folded through a dressing. The flooded fields double as crawfish ponds once the rice is cut.

On our menus rice is the popcorn rice under the Seafood Gumbo, an aromatic long grain with its own card, and the base of the South Louisiana Rice Dressing. The rice grits under the Blackened Tofu are from Two Brooks Farm in Mississippi, not Louisiana.

The dressing prints no description, so whose rice it is, and which meats go in, are learned at lineup.

Blanching is a short plunge into boiling salted water, and shocking is the plunge into iced water that follows, which stops the cooking at once. The heat kills the enzymes that would dull a green vegetable, so a blanched green keeps its colour and its bite for days, and the ice keeps it from cooking on in its own heat. Blanched food is finished later, squeezed, sautéed, fried or sauced, which is why restaurants do it: the long part of the work happens before service.

On our menus the classic method behind the creamed spinach, under the Eggs Sardou and as a side, is spinach blanched, shocked, squeezed hard and chopped before the cream, and Brabant potatoes, on the breakfast side and the children's plates, start as cubes blanched or par-fried before their final crisping.

Whether ours are made that way, and which vegetables the kitchen blanches ahead on a given night, are the chef's answers, never a guess.

Dried pasta is cooked in a large pot of well salted boiling water, stirred at the start so it does not stick, and pulled when it is al dente, firm to the bite with no chalky centre. A shape with a hollow, like a shell, is drained but not rinsed, because the starch left on its surface helps a sauce cling, and a little of the cooking water loosens a cheese sauce that has tightened. Pasta that will be finished in a sauce comes out a minute early, since it keeps cooking in the heat.

On our menus the Shells & Cheese folds pasta shells into a beer and cheese fondue, and the children's dinner tosses buttered noodles with cheese.

Whether the shells are cooked to order or held and reheated for service is the kitchen's method, not printed, so ask the chef. Pasta is wheat. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

The lemon is a citrus thought to have begun in India, growing in southern Italy by about the year 200 and now planted almost entirely in California and Arizona for the American crop, mostly as Eureka and Lisbon, two varieties of the same sharp, thin-skinned fruit. The juice's acid is almost all citric, the cook's cleanest sourness, and the zest holds the oils that carry the perfume.

A squeeze wakes a sauce, a curd or a jelly; salted and cured for weeks, the peel turns soft and savoury as preserved lemon.

Lemon is printed on five of our plates: the lemon curd in the Blackberry Trifle, the lemon in the Crab & Corn Omelette, the preserved lemon in the Redfish Véronique's beurre blanc and on the Smoked Cauliflower with harissa, and the lemon jelly in the Lemon Tart. Which lemons the kitchen buys is a question for the chef.
