Nicolas Feuillatte is the brand of a growers’ cooperative group at Chouilly, near Épernay. The Centre Vinicole de la Champagne, a group of cooperatives, was founded in 1972 so growers could pool their wine and their sales. Nicolas Feuillatte, a Parisian who built a business in the United States importing African coffee, launched his own Champagne in 1976, and in 1986 the brand passed to the Centre Vinicole.

At the end of 2021 the cooperative merged with Castelnau’s to form Terroirs et Vignerons de Champagne, about 6,000 growers. The house blend, Réserve Exclusive Brut, which our list prints as Réserve, is 40 percent Pinot Noir, 40 percent Meunier and 20 percent Chardonnay: fresh, fruity and easy.

Our half-bottle is $65, a Champagne for two at brunch and the pick for the Eggs Hussarde.

Paul Bara is a family grower in Bouzy, a grand cru village of the Montagne de Reims famous for Pinot Noir. The family has been in Bouzy since 1833 by most sources, and Paul Bara was the first to sell Champagne under his own name, from the 1950s. As a récoltant-manipulant it makes Champagne only from its own grand cru vines, mostly Pinot Noir, so the wines are full and red-fruited. It belongs to the Club Trésors de Champagne, whose Special Club wines must pass a tasting panel twice.

On Birthday Bubbles we pour its rosé in a half-bottle: about 80 percent Pinot Noir, part of it Bouzy’s own still red wine for colour, and 20 percent Chardonnay. The bottle list adds the Extra Brut and the Special Club white and rosé.

The Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, which guests call DRC, is in Vosne-Romanée and for many collectors the most celebrated wine estate in the world. It owns two grand crus outright, Romanée-Conti and La Tâche, both monopoles, holds parcels of Richebourg, Romanée-Saint-Vivant, Grands-Échezeaux and Échezeaux, farms Corton, and makes the whites Le Montrachet and Corton-Charlemagne.

The Romanée-Conti vineyard takes its name from the Prince de Conti, who bought it in 1760. The domaine dates from 1869, and since 1942 it has been run as a société civile by the de Villaine and Leroy families. Its reds are made with whole bunches and long ageing in new oak: perfume and lift rather than weight.

We carry the Échezeaux 2015, La Tâche 2012 and Romanée-Conti 2014 among many vintages. Recognise the request, confirm the bottle and bring the sommelier.

Domaine Armand Rousseau is the family domaine at the head of nearly every list for Gevrey-Chambertin. Armand Rousseau built it in the early twentieth century, and in the 1930s it was among the estates that pioneered bottling and selling under their own name, when most Burgundy still left the cellar in cask for a merchant.

Its grand crus include Chambertin, Chambertin-Clos de Bèze, the walled monopole Clos des Ruchottes, Mazis-Chambertin and Charmes-Chambertin. It also holds the largest share of the premier cru Clos Saint-Jacques, which many rank beside the grand crus. The grapes are destemmed, and the wines are deep and savoury, built on tannin and length.

Our bottle is the Clos Saint-Jacques 2019, bin 23651. It is young: suggest a decant and bring the sommelier.

In the 1930s it was one of the estates that pioneered domaine bottling: it bottled and sold wine under its own name when most Burgundy still left the cellar in cask for a merchant to raise and label. His son Charles Rousseau carried the domaine on.

The holdings read like a map of Gevrey’s best ground. There are parcels of Chambertin and Chambertin-Clos de Bèze, the two crus at the head of the village’s nine grand crus; the Clos des Ruchottes, a walled monopole inside Ruchottes-Chambertin; and Mazis-Chambertin and Charmes-Chambertin. There is also the premier cru Clos Saint-Jacques, routinely argued to deserve grand cru rank. It has five owners, and Rousseau holds the largest share.

Fattoria di Fèlsina farms at Castelnuovo Berardenga, the southern extremity of Chianti Classico, northeast of Siena, where the zone meets the clay hills of the Crete Senesi. Chianti Classico is the historic heart of Chianti between Florence and Siena, and this corner is warmer and drier than the northern communes. Fèlsina's Sangiovese is firm, savoury and mineral, with oak in support rather than for flavour. The Codex dates the estate from 1966.

Fèlsina is a Sangiovese house. Its Chianti Classico is all Sangiovese, fermented in stainless steel and aged about twelve months in medium-size Slavonian oak casks; in some markets it is labelled Berardenga. Rancia, a parcel on a former monastic site, is bottled on its own as a Chianti Classico Riserva and is the reference for southern Chianti Classico. Fontalloro, pure Sangiovese from parcels on both sides of the DOCG boundary, must be labelled IGT for geography alone, and Colonia, a Gran Selezione, is the estate's most structured wine.

Our list prints four: the Chianti Classico 2022 at $90, the Rancia Riserva 2019 and 2020 at $165 each, and Maestro Raro 2019, which the wine list calls their Cabernet, among the Super Tuscans.

Gaja is the family winery in the village of Barbaresco, in the Langhe hills of Piedmont, dated by the Codex to 1859. Angelo Gaja made it one of the most famous names in Italian wine and took Barbaresco from the lesser neighbour of Barolo to a wine priced above it.

From the 1960s, beginning with Sorì San Lorenzo, Gaja put single vineyard names on Barbaresco labels, bottling Sorì San Lorenzo, Sorì Tildìn and Costa Russi on their own in a region that blended by tradition. Sorì is Piedmontese for a south-facing slope, and Tildìn was Angelo's grandmother Clotilde. From the 1996 vintage the three were labelled Langhe Nebbiolo, so Barbera could be blended in; with 2013, a return the Codex credits to Angelo's daughter Gaia, they went back to Barbaresco. Darmagi, Cabernet planted in the Langhe, is named for his father's dismay.

The style is polished: low yields, rigorous selection and French oak, dark-fruited Nebbiolo with international reach. The house later bought land in Barolo and in Tuscany, and the Gaja name is also on Pieve Santa Restituta in Montalcino and Ca' Marcanda near Bolgheri.

Ours is the flagship Barbaresco 2012 at $380, bin 16332, all Nebbiolo from the family's vineyards in the village.

Biondi Santi is the family credited with creating Brunello di Montalcino, at Tenuta Greppo, outside the hill town of Montalcino south of Siena. In the nineteenth century Ferruccio Biondi Santi propagated a selection of Sangiovese known locally as Brunello, the little dark one, and his late-1800s bottlings are the reference for what pure Sangiovese in Montalcino means. The estate's own selection, BBS11, carries the name on. Brunello's rules, all Sangiovese and five years of ageing, six for a Riserva, descend from what this house was already doing.

The Greppo lies south-east of the town at roughly 500 metres, cooled by altitude. The style is pale, high-toned and acid-driven, aged in large old Slavonian casks with no new oak and built to be unapproachable young. The Riserva comes only from the oldest parcels and only in outstanding years, and old bottles are called back to the cellar to be topped up and recorked, so the library reaches into the nineteenth century. The Annata is the regular Brunello of the year, and the Rosso di Montalcino the younger wine.

In December 2016 the EPI group of the Descours family, which also owns Piper-Heidsieck, Charles Heidsieck and Rare Champagne, acquired the majority of the estate. Jacopo Biondi Santi's Castello di Montepo wines are a separate operation.

Ours is the Annata 2012 at $425, bin 18542.

changes.before:
Masseto is pure Merlot from a single hill of blue clay at Bolgheri, on the Tuscan coast. The clay holds water through the hot coastal summer, which is why Merlot behaves there as it does nowhere else in Tuscany; the Codex calls it Italy's answer to Pétrus. The vineyard was first planted by Tenuta dell'Ornellaia, the estate Lodovico Antinori founded in 1981, and Masseto's first vintage was 1986. It is now run as a separate estate with its own cellar, and it is labelled Toscana IGT, not Bolgheri DOC.

Ours is the 2011 at $1080, fifteen years old. The list prints it under Tenuta dell'Ornellaia, with 2015, 2016 and 2020 beside it.

changes.before:
Opus One is the partnership that told the world Napa had arrived. Robert Mondavi, whose Oakville winery of 1966 led the valley's reinvention, and Baron Philippe de Rothschild of Château Mouton Rothschild, the Pauillac first growth, agreed at the end of the 1970s to make one wine together: the first serious joint venture between a Bordeaux first growth proprietor and a New World producer. The Codex reads it as the commercial consequence of the Paris tasting, when European houses began to treat Napa as a place to invest.

The first vintage was 1979, released in 1984 together with the 1980, and it was priced from the start at a level no Californian bottle had attempted. The estate is in Oakville, with vineyards that include land beside the historic To Kalon vineyard, first planted by H.W. Crabb in 1868, and a purpose-built winery completed in 1991. Opus One is its own winery and brand, not a Robert Mondavi bottling, and it is even sold through La Place de Bordeaux, the city's merchant network.

The wine is a Cabernet Sauvignon-led blend with the other Bordeaux grapes, aged in new French oak: Bordeaux proportion applied to Napa fruit, cassis and cedar, polish before power. Overture is the second wine. Our list runs from half-bottles to a six litre bottle; we study the 2015 half-bottle and the 2010.

Screaming Eagle is the defining name of Napa's cult era. Jean Phillips bought a small property on the eastern side of the Oakville valley floor in 1986; the first vintage, 1992, was made by Heidi Barrett and released in 1995. Caymus Vineyards is the Rutherford winery the Wagner family founded: the Codex dates it to 1972 and calls it Charlie Wagner's house. The name comes from the Rancho Caymus land grant: Caymus is a producer, not an appellation.

It is among the most widely sold serious Napa Cabernets in America and the clearest example of the ripe, sweet-fruited Napa style: cassis, vanilla and soft, plush tannin, with a finish that reads faintly sweet though the wine is dry. The Napa Valley Cabernet draws fruit from across the valley, not only from Rutherford, and the Codex credits it with setting the modern popular Napa taste. Special Selection is the reserve, from the best lots and aged longer in oak. Randy Dunn made the wines here and founded Dunn Vineyards on Howell Mountain.

Belle Glos, a Pinot Noir label on our list, Mer Soleil and Conundrum are other Wagner family labels, not Caymus wines. Our list prints the Napa Valley 2023, the Special Selection 2018, a Special Select magnum of 2019 and a 50th Anniversary bottling in a three litre bottle.

Chappellet was founded in 1967, when Donn and Molly Chappellet came to Pritchard Hill, in the eastern hills of the Napa Valley above the valley floor. It was a year after Robert Mondavi broke ground at Oakville, and the Chappellets were pioneers of the slope, there long before the cult producers now associated with it.

Pritchard Hill is famous, but it is not an appellation, so wines from the hill are labelled Napa Valley. The vineyards are steep and rocky, and the wines show it: dried herb, red currant and a firm, gritty tannin rather than cult polish.

Three Chappellet reds are on our list. Pritchard Hill is the estate flagship, from the original hillside blocks; Signature is the long-running house Cabernet; Mountain Cuvée is the friendliest, a Cabernet-led Bordeaux-style blend drawn from the estate and other Napa vineyards, the mix changing every year. Chappellet also makes a dry Chenin Blanc, a grape now rare in Napa.

Ours by the bottle is the Mountain Cuvée 2024, our Napa red under $100: black cherry, cassis and mocha, soft and ready now.

Frog's Leap is John Williams's winery in Rutherford, in the middle of the Napa Valley; Larry Turley, later of Turley Wine Cellars, was its co-founder. It is known for farming organically and for dry farming: the vines get no irrigation and send their roots deep for water, a deliberate choice in a West where irrigation is routine. The wines are balanced and lower in alcohol than many Napa reds.

The Estate Rutherford Cabernet comes from its own vineyards on Rutherford's valley floor, home of the dusty tannin André Tchelistcheff called Rutherford dust. Ours is the 2021, fresh and savoury, with the 2020 and a 1991 also on the list: Napa for the guest who wants it fresh rather than heavy.

Silver Oak Cellars was founded in 1972 by Justin Meyer, who had learned winemaking as one of the Christian Brothers, and Ray Duncan.

From the start it has done one thing. Silver Oak makes only Cabernet Sauvignon, in two bottlings, Napa Valley and Alexander Valley, ages them only in American oak, and rests them in bottle before release. American oak gives a more overt vanilla than French, and far more of the lactone that reads as coconut and dill, so the house style is easy to recognise: ripe dark fruit, sweet spice and a smooth, polished texture. Many guests ask for it by name.

The two valleys give two characters. Alexander Valley, in Sonoma, runs north from Healdsburg beyond the reach of most of the fog, and its Cabernet is softer and earlier drinking; the Napa Valley bottling is the firmer of the two.

Our list prints both: the Napa Valley 2020, the bottle with its own card, and the Alexander Valley 2021 at half its price. The Napa 2020 is a first pick for the Roost Burger, a name to toast with and the weight for double short rib, bacon and cheese, and just as happy with a steak.

Broadbent is a label rather than a lodge. Bartholomew Broadbent is a British wine merchant and Madeira specialist, the founder of Broadbent Selections and an importer of Madeira into North America, and he bottles Madeira under his own name. Wine Spectator lists the Broadbent Madeiras under Justino's, one of the island's producers.

His single cask bottlings are drawn from one cask of one harvest, so each is a little different. Ours is the Malvasia 2009, aged in old 650 litre oak casks and bottled in 500 ml. Malvasia, or Malmsey, is Madeira's sweetest style, kept tangy by the island's high natural acidity: coffee, caramel, toffee and orange peel. The list also prints a drier Single Cask Verdelho 1997.

Madeira needs no decanting and keeps for months once opened.

Maison Joseph Drouhin is one of the great family houses of Beaune, founded in 1880 and named for Joseph Drouhin, with its cellars under the town. It is both a merchant house and a grower, with vineyards of its own across the Côte d’Or and in Chablis, farmed organically and biodynamically. Its style is light-handed and aromatic, with modest new oak: elegance in preference to weight.

Its signature is the Clos des Mouches, a premier cru on the slope above Beaune, where Drouhin owns the largest share and makes the wine in both colours, red and white. It also farms and sells the Montrachet of the Marquis de Laguiche, whose family owns the parcel, and the wine list carries its Musigny and its Chambolle-Musigny Les Amoureuses.

The name reaches Oregon too. In 1980 Robert Drouhin organised a rematch of the 1979 Gault-Millau tasting in Paris, and in the rematch The Eyrie Vineyards’ 1975 South Block, an Oregon Pinot Noir, placed second. In 1987 he bought land in Oregon’s Dundee Hills and founded Domaine Drouhin Oregon, with his daughter Véronique as winemaker.

Our bottle is the red Clos des Mouches 2015, eleven years old: red and black cherry, rose and spice, silky tannin.

Domaine Georges Roumier is a family domaine in Chambolle-Musigny, founded in 1924, and one of the most sought-after names in Burgundy. Its wines are drawn fine and cool: red currant, crushed rock and rose, with restrained oak and a stony finish. Its grand crus, among them Bonnes-Mares and a sliver of Musigny, and its premier cru Les Amoureuses are hard to find anywhere.

The Clos de la Bussière is a walled premier cru in neighbouring Morey-Saint-Denis that Roumier owns alone, a monopole, and it shows a darker, earthier side of the house than its Chambolle-Musigny wines. Ours is the 2014, the celebration bottle for the Blackened Tofu.

René Rostaing's domaine is at Ampuis, the village beneath the steep terraces of Côte-Rôtie, the roasted slope at the northern end of the Rhône valley, where Syrah grows at its most perfumed. Each is picked late and raised around forty-two months in new oak, far longer than the appellation's habit.

Our La Mouline 2012 has fourteen years: violet, raspberry and blackberry, bacon and spice, with a long, fine finish.

Château Rayas is the Reynaud family's estate in Châteauneuf-du-Pape, dated by the Codex to 1880, and it is the appellation's great exception. Most Châteauneuf is a blend grown over hot, round stones; Rayas lies in the cool, wooded north-east of the appellation on sand and clay, without galets, and its red is Grenache alone.

Sand, the shade of the surrounding pine woods and very low yields give a wine so pale and perfumed that it is regularly mistaken for red Burgundy when tasted blind. It is raised in old wood, with no new oak and no pretence of power: kirsch, incense and red fruit rather than the dark warmth of its neighbours. Rayas is why examiners say Châteauneuf need not be a blend and need not be dark.

Jacques Reynaud ran the estate until his death in 1997, and his nephew Emmanuel Reynaud followed him; our wine list of October 2026 names Emmanuel as the hand behind Rayas and Château des Tours.

The family's other wines are on our list too: Pignan, a named parcel of the same estate; Château de Fonsalette and La Pialade, both Côtes du Rhône; and Château des Tours in Vacqueyras. Rayas itself appears in three vintages. Ours is the 2011, fifteen years old, translucent and silky.

Do Ferreiro is a grower in the Val do Salnés, the coolest and most maritime of the five subzones of Rías Baixas, on the Atlantic coast of Galicia. The Codex names the grower Gerardo Méndez and places the estate's small granite parcels around Meaño. Ferreiro is Galician for blacksmith.

The Sparr name in Alsace goes back to 1680, the year the house gives for Jean Sparr in the village of Sigolsheim; some sources call it the founding, others his birth, and one guide dates the family's vines to 1634. Pierre Sparr, who gave the house its name, took over in the early 1900s at about twenty and, by the house's account, became one of the pioneers of estate bottling in Alsace. In 2009 the house was taken over by the Cave de Beblenheim, a cooperative founded in 1952 near Riquewihr, which keeps the Pierre Sparr name; the house now stands on the cooperative's street in Beblenheim, and its importer describes fruit from member growers. The range still includes grand cru wines from the Mambourg, the south-facing slope of Mount Sigolsheim, and the Schoenenbourg between Riquewihr and Zellenberg.

At Brennan's the Sparr is the pink bubbles by the glass: a Crémant d'Alsace Brut Rosé, all Pinot Noir, made by the traditional method and aged at least 18 months on its lees by the importer's sheet. The list also carries Sparr's Mambourg and Schoenenbourg grand crus from 2020.

Jansz is named for the Dutch explorer Abel Janszoon Tasman, who sighted the island in 1642. Its vineyard at Pipers River, in the north-east of Tasmania, was established in 1975 and first carried the name Heemskerk, after Tasman's ship.

In 1986 Heemskerk Wines and the Champagne house Louis Roederer, which had recognised how closely the Tasmanian climate resembled Champagne's, joined forces there to make sparkling wine; one source dates the partnership to 1982. In 1989, by one account, the estate made Tasmania's first sparkling wine by the traditional method. The Hill-Smith family, owners of Yalumba, bought the label and vineyard in 1998 by most accounts and renamed it Jansz Tasmania.

Pipers River is cool and close to the sea: breezes off the Bass Strait keep winters mild and summers cool, so the grapes ripen slowly and keep their acidity. Jansz calls its approach méthode Tasmanoise, to stress the island rather than imitate Champagne, though the method is the same second fermentation in bottle.

The house's non-vintage is the Premium Cuvée, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from several Tasmanian vineyards. Our list prints Jansz Premier Cuvée Brut 2022 at $65, the first pick for the Creole Spiced Nuts, so the sommelier should confirm which bottling is in the cellar.

Domaine Raymond Dupont-Fahn is a small family estate near Meursault. Hachette and two merchants place it at Tailly, a little village on the plain just south of Meursault; other Hachette entries describe a Dupont-Fahn domaine at Monthélie, next door, and whether that is the same business is not settled. Merchants date the estate to 1975, but they disagree on which grandfather made the first purchase and on how many generations have run it since, so the honest line is a small family domaine.

Its best-known wine is Les Tillets. The vineyard is a lieu-dit, a named village site, at the top of the Meursault slope: one of the highest in Meursault, with rocky topsoil, and its height gives the wine an unusual freshness. By its merchant, the 2022 is all Chardonnay with about a fifth new oak, from a family that favours early harvests, organic farming and no chaptalisation.

The other story guests enjoy is Chaumes des Perrières. By the merchants’ accounts, the family’s rocky land on the boundary of Perrières and Sous le Dos d’Ane was judged too thin in the 1970s, and the INAO allowed 20 cm of topsoil to be spread on it; neighbouring growers objected, and the parcel was declassified from Meursault to Bourgogne.

Domaine Paul Pillot is a family estate in Chassagne-Montrachet. One merchant’s history traces the family’s vines in the village to 1900, when a cooper turned to growing grapes; other sources begin the story with Paul Pillot himself.

Paul Pillot took charge in 1968 and expanded the holdings, which include the Chassagne premiers crus Clos Saint-Jean, Grandes Ruchottes and Caillerets. His son Thierry joined in 1999 and has run the domaine since 2004 by most accounts, 2007 by one; Thierry’s sister Chrystelle joined a few years later, and the fourth generation splits the work, Chrystelle in the vineyards and Thierry in the cellar. Thierry also has a small négoce label of his own, listed separately on our wine list.

The vines lie mostly in Chassagne-Montrachet, Saint-Aubin and Santenay, with small parcels in neighbouring villages. Both of the family’s Saint-Aubin vineyards sit on the east-facing hillside bordering the Chassagne premier cru Les Chaumées, cut off from the rest of Saint-Aubin by a small valley. Le Charmois, our bottle, comes from vines over 50 years old on marl and limestone soils rich in iron, raised with only about a tenth new oak, so the wine stays crisp and chalky: Chassagne’s neighbour at a gentler price.

Domaine Coche-Dury of Meursault makes some of the scarcest and most coveted white wine in the world. Léon Coche began buying vines in Meursault, Auxey-Duresses and Monthélie in 1923; his grandson Jean-François, Georges’s son, took over in the early 1970s and added his wife Odile Dury’s name. Robert Parker’s praise in the 1980s made it famous, and their son Raphaël Coche has made the wines since his father retired in 2010.

The style rests on long lees ageing in barrel with regular stirring, which gives the struck-match, flinty edge over citrus and a saline finish. Our Bourgogne Blanc 2022, $690, is the estate’s regional white, from parcels scattered through its Meursault vines by a merchant’s account: priced for its scarcity, not its appellation.

In the 1980s Robert Parker’s praise made him famous, and Coche-Dury became the reference for a reductive style of white Burgundy: long ageing on the lees in barrel, regular bâtonnage and a struck-match, flinty edge over citrus and a saline finish. Sotheby’s notes that recent vintages show a gentler struck match and gunflint.

Their son Raphaël Coche joined full time in the late 1990s and took over the winemaking when his father retired in 2010. In a Decanter profile he argues that everything in Meursault is under-classified, a village with no grand cru at all.

Domaine du Pélican is the Jura estate of the d'Angerville family, whose Domaine Marquis d'Angerville in Volnay is one of the great names of Burgundy: Sem d'Angerville was one of the growers who forced estate bottling and helped build the appellation system in the 1930s. The family founded the Jura estate in 2012, and it is a separate property, at Arbois.

Arbois is the Jura's largest appellation and was among the first French appellations, granted in 1936. The Jura makes its whites two ways. Ouillé wines are topped up in barrel like any other white. Sous voile wines are left untopped, so a veil of yeast grows on the surface and gives a nutty, savoury, sherry-like tang.

Vin Jaune is the purest sous voile wine: Savagnin alone, aged in cask without topping up for at least six years and three months, sixty months of it under the veil, and sold only in the squat 62 cl clavelin. It is never fortified; it finishes at ordinary table-wine strength.

The Pélican range on our list shows both faces of the Jura: the Grand Curoulet Chardonnay and the Savagnin Ouillé, topped up and fresh; a sparkling S°; two reds; and the Vin Jaune 2016, the bottle in our pairings, chosen to mirror the aged sherry that finishes the turtle soup.

Pommery was founded in Reims in 1858 as Pommery & Greno by Alexandre Louis Pommery and Narcisse Greno, at first as a wool business; one source dates the firm to 1836. Widowed, Louise Pommery took control, sold the wool trade and gave the house to Champagne.

She built it twice over. Under Reims she bought some 120 Gallo-Roman chalk pits, the crayères, for her cellars, beneath an estate begun in 1868. And in 1874 she launched Pommery Nature, the first brut Champagne to succeed commercially, when most Champagne was very sweet; the dry style the English took to became the world’s taste. By one account the house sold in about 80 countries by her death in 1890.

Pommery has belonged to the Vranken-Pommery group since 2002. Its Brut Rosé Royal blends the three grapes in near-equal shares by a 2022 competition entry, and takes its colour, by a merchant’s account, from red wine of Bouzy Pinot Noir.

Louis Pommery is the group’s sparkling wine from California, on sale in American cities by 2017 and named for the house’s founder. It is made by the traditional method from grapes chosen across California; one source gives the Brut Rosé as 76 percent Chardonnay and 24 percent Pinot Noir. It is not Champagne.

Franz Hirtzberger is a family estate at Spitz in the Wachau, the narrow, terraced gorge of the Danube west of Krems that makes many of Austria's greatest dry whites. Spitz lies upriver, in the western part of the valley.

The estate is one of the names that define the Wachau. Its two most famous vineyards are the Honivogl, its great Grüner Veltliner site, and the Singerriedel, the Riesling site the Codex pairs with Hirtzberger among the Wachau's leading rieds. Both are on our list as Smaragd.

Smaragd belongs to Vinea Wachau, the growers' association founded in 1983, which sorts its members' dry wines by ripeness: Steinfeder, the lightest, then Federspiel, then Smaragd, the ripest and fullest, at 12.5 per cent alcohol or more, named for the emerald lizard that suns itself on the terrace walls. The words are the association's trademarks, not Austrian law, and appear only on Wachau labels; its Codex Wachau forbids chaptalisation and concentration. Since the 2020 vintage the Wachau has also been a DAC.

Our Honivogl Smaragd 2022 is Grüner Veltliner at its grandest: ripe pear, quince, white pepper, honeyed spice and stone, rich and powerful yet dry. A separate Wachau grower, Mathias Hirtzberger, is also on the list; the list says only that he comes from the Hirtzberger family.

Jean Foillard farms old Gamay vines at Villié-Morgon, in the Morgon cru of Beaujolais. With Marcel Lapierre, Jean-Paul Thévenet and Guy Breton he belongs to the group their American importer, Kermit Lynch, called the Gang of Four. They followed the oenologist Jules Chauvet back to whole bunches, native yeasts and little or no added sulphur at a time when much Beaujolais was industrial, and their Morgon became a root of the natural wine movement.

His name is tied to the Côte du Py, the hill at the heart of Morgon, whose decomposed schist sets it apart from the granite of most Beaujolais crus. Foillard also farms Corcelette, a sandier granite site that gives a lighter, more floral Morgon, and vines in Fleurie.

Marcel Lapierre was the central figure of the Beaujolais natural wine movement. From his family domaine at Villié-Morgon he worked, with Jean Foillard, Jean-Paul Thévenet and Guy Breton, from the teaching of Jules Chauvet, a Beaujolais négociant and research chemist whose work on native yeasts and minimal sulphur shaped their generation. Their American importer, Kermit Lynch, called the four the Gang of Four.

At a time when much Beaujolais was industrial, sugared and fermented with cultured yeast, Lapierre went back to old vines, whole bunches and the grapes’ own yeasts. The wines are made by whole-bunch semi-carbonic fermentation with indigenous yeasts, no chaptalisation and little or no added sulphur, from old Gamay vines farmed without herbicides, including parcels on the Côte du Py.

Ridge Vineyards was founded in 1962 high in the Santa Cruz Mountains, south of San Francisco, at Monte Bello, where Osea Perrone had built a winery in the 1880s. The vineyard climbs to about 800 metres on a limestone-bearing ridge above the San Andreas fault, and its Cabernet-led blend, Monte Bello, became one of America's great wines under Paul Draper, Ridge's longtime winemaker.

On 24 May 1976 the Monte Bello 1971 came fifth among the reds at the Paris tasting; thirty years later, at the anniversary re-tasting of 24 May 2006, held in London and Napa at once, it came first.

We pour six: Monte Bello 2012, the Estate Cabernet half from the Monte Bello vineyards, Lytton Springs in bottle and in half, Three Valleys, and Essence, a sweet late harvest Zinfandel made only in exceptional years.

Dow's is one of the great Port houses of the Douro valley in northern Portugal. The Codex gives its founding year as 1798, and notes that Dow's is the brand while Silva and Cosens is the company behind it.

In 1882 a young Scot, Andrew James Symington, came to Porto to work for Graham's. He became a partner in Warre's and, in 1912, in Dow's. The Symington family runs Dow's today alongside Graham's, Warre's and Cockburn's, as of October 2026.

Dow's home estate is Quinta do Bomfim at Pinhão, in the Cima Corgo, the heart of the Port vineyards, and the Codex adds Quinta da Senhora da Ribeira in the hotter Douro Superior. In years without a declaration, both are bottled on their own as single quinta Vintage Ports.

The house style is the thing to remember. Dow's Vintage Ports finish drier than most, firm and savoury, because the house leaves less sugar in the wine; Graham's, from the same family, is richer and sweeter. Dry here is relative: every Vintage Port is a sweet wine.

We pour two declared vintages: the 2000 in a half-bottle and the 1985, now forty-one years old.

Sandeman is one of the oldest names in Port. George Sandeman, a Scot, founded it in London in 1790 to ship Port and sherry, the fortified wines of Portugal and of Spain.

Its fame today rests as much on a picture as on a wine. In 1928 the artist George Massiot Brown drew the Don, a figure in silhouette wearing a Portuguese student's cape and a wide Spanish hat. The Codex explains the pairing: the house sold both Port and sherry and wanted one mark to carry the two. The Don is called the oldest wine logo still in use, and the Codex records it in unbroken use since 1928. Guests recognise it at once.

Our list prints two Sandeman wines. Ours in the pairings is the Late Bottled Vintage 1999: Port from a single year, kept four to six years in wood before bottling, and since then more than two decades in bottle, so it is mellow and mature, with dark cherry, plum, fig and spice.

The other is printed simply as Sandeman 1977, which the house's own notes treat as a Vintage Port: a different wine that throws a crust, so ring by vintage and bin.

Domaine de l’Écu is at Le Landreau, in Muscadet Sèvre et Maine near Nantes, the western end of the Loire where the weather comes off the Atlantic. Muscadet is the appellation and Melon de Bourgogne the grape, and Sèvre et Maine names two small rivers that drain the heart of the vineyard.

The estate farms biodynamically and is long associated with Guy Bossard, an early champion of organic and then biodynamic farming in Muscadet. Its idea is simple and rare: the vines of one grape in one village are bottled by the rock beneath them. Granite gives the ripest and roundest wine, Gneiss the most floral, and Orthogneiss, a gneiss formed from an igneous rock such as granite, the tightest and most saline, the estate’s usual benchmark. Gneiss weathers into a poor, stony soil that holds almost no water, so the vines root deep and crop lightly. Many of the wines are made with little or no added sulphur.

That makes it the clearest teaching example in France of soil-named wines from a single grape, and a standing argument against Muscadet as a cheap category.

Ours is the Orthogneiss 2022 at $70, printed Domaine L’Ecu, the value bottle for the Creole Caesar. The estate’s Pinot Noir, Ange, sold as Vin de France, is on our red list at $135.

Domaine de la Pépière is at Maisdon-sur-Sèvre, in Muscadet Sèvre et Maine near Nantes. Marc Ollivier founded it in 1984 and farmed organically from the start, and it became the estate that made Muscadet serious again.

Its secret is time. Ordinary Muscadet sur lie rests on its lees through one winter and is bottled the year after the harvest; Pépière took lees ageing far beyond the legal minimum, for salt, citrus pith and stony grip, with no oak and no fruit gloss. Its old vines on granite give the Clos des Briords, the bottling that made Muscadet collectable.

Ours is the Monnières-Saint Fiacre 2020 at $75, the value bottle for the Grand Isle Jewel Oysters. The list also prints it in magnum, and a Château-Thébaud 2019 magnum.

Domaine des Baumard is a family estate at Rochefort-sur-Loire, in Anjou; the Codex dates it to 1955. It is the estate that carries both faces of Anjou Chenin Blanc, so it answers the appellation question from either side.

On the north bank it has parcels in Savennières, including the Clos du Papillon, a celebrated lieu-dit shared by more than one owner, for dry, taut Chenin. Across the river it has holdings in Quarts de Chaume, a tiny south-facing amphitheatre of schist above the Layon and the Loire’s only grand cru, for sweet wine. The Layon valley draws noble rot in the best years, and Chenin’s searching acidity carries great sweetness without turning cloying, which is why a sweet Layon still tastes fresh after decades.

The house style is technically precise and clean, with acidity preserved and sweetness carried lightly. The Clos Sainte Catherine is its Coteaux du Layon at moderate sweetness, a bridge between the dry and the botrytised styles.

Ours is the Clos Sainte Catherine 2006 at $90, twenty years old: quince, baked apple, honey, apricot and a little ginger, the value bottle for the Baked Apple and the New Orleans Bread Pudding. The estate’s dry Savennières 2018 is on the list at $85.

Domaine de Châteaumar is a Southern Rhône estate, and the wine we know is its Cuvée Vincent, the red on the Traditional Breakfast at Brennan's: a 4 oz pour with the Petite Filet Mignon, included in the tasting, with no glass price on the list.

Its story is in the vineyard. The Cuvée Vincent comes from old Syrah, fifty year old vines by published accounts, on two parcels bordering Châteauneuf-du-Pape, about nine kilometres from Orange, farmed organically without certification. It is sold as Côtes du Rhône, the regional name, rather than Châteauneuf, and it is all Syrah, which is the talking point: in the Southern Rhône the reds are usually blends led by Grenache. An early guide called it Grenache-based; accounts of the 2016 and 2022 vintages describe it as all Syrah, so it is never called Grenache.

Creekstone Farms began in 1995, when John and Carol Stewart set up a purebred Black Angus farm in Campbellsburg, Kentucky. Stewart was a cattle geneticist at heart: he developed his own Angus line, sold bulls, genetics and semen to ranchers, and at one point owned the highest-marbling bull in the breed.

In 2003 the company moved into processing, buying a processing plant in Arkansas City, Kansas, where it began processing its own Premium Black Angus cattle in May 2003. Its cattle-receiving facility was the first built from the ground up to the low-stress handling standards of Dr. Temple Grandin. After BSE was found in the US herd in December 2003, Creekstone asked in 2004 to test every animal it slaughtered, and when the USDA refused, it took the question to court.

Stewart announced his retirement in October 2006. Sun Capital Partners had owned the business since 2005, and in 2017 it sold Creekstone to the Japanese trading house Marubeni Corporation, which owns it today. The company still buys its cattle on verifiable Black Angus genetics rather than hide colour, and its Natural Black Angus line carries the Certified Humane label.

At Brennan's the name is printed on three plates: both hanger steaks and the tenderloin of the Roasted Chateaubriand.

The Rohan is D'Artagnan's own duck. D'Artagnan was founded in 1985 by Ariane Daguin and George Faison, who met working at a charcuterie shop in New York City. A farmer had the first domestically raised foie gras in the United States and needed someone to sell it, so the two started a company to do it, selling whole raw lobes to New York chefs. Daguin was born in Auch, in Gascony, the eldest child of the Michelin-starred chef André Daguin, and the company is named for the Gascon musketeer. It is based in Union, New Jersey.

D'Artagnan's blog introduced the Rohan in January 2012. It is a proprietary cross of several breeds, including the heritage Mallard and the Pekin, bred to approximate a style of duck found in Normandy and named for the family of dukes and princes of Rohan in Brittany. The birds are raised for D'Artagnan on a farm in New York's Catskills, cage-free and never given antibiotics, hormones or steroids, to 11 weeks, five weeks longer than the average factory duck. Daguin says the extra time deepens the flavour and improves the meat-to-bone ratio.

The result is rosy, tender, mild meat with a rich, buttery depth. Brennan's prints Rohan on the duck breast of the dinner tasting and on the confit leg of the Duck Confit Waffle.

Grana Padano traces itself to 1135 and the Abbey of Chiaravalle, a few kilometres south of Milan. Bernard of Clairvaux had chosen to reclaim the marshland there, and his Cistercian monks drained and farmed it. With more milk than they could drink, they made a hard cheese that kept, which they called caseus vetus, old cheese. Ordinary people named it for its texture instead: grana, grainy, and Padano, from the Po Valley.

The Consorzio di Tutela, which protects the name, was founded on 18 June 1954, uniting producers, refiners and merchants, and the European Union made Grana Padano a DOP in 1996. Every wheel, 24 to 40 kg, ages at least nine months; at nine months inspectors test it with a hammer, a needle and a probe, and only a wheel that passes is fire-branded. Some age beyond 24 months.

It is now the world's best-selling protected cheese, over 5.2 million wheels in 2022. Its rules are its own: it may be made in 32 provinces across five northern regions, the cows may eat silage, and lysozyme, a protein from egg white, may be used as a preservative. With its nine-month minimum it is a younger, milder and different cheese from Parmigiano Reggiano, not a lesser copy of it.

Mimolette is the French answer to Dutch Edam. The story told in France is that Louis XIV, under the mercantilist policies of his minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert, wanted a native cheese to replace the Edam the French were buying. Another telling has Colbert's embargo on foreign goods leaving the people of Flanders without their favourite Dutch-style cheese, so they made it themselves. Either way, it was made around Lille, and to tell it apart from Edam it was coloured, first with carrot juice and later with annatto, the seed that gives its blazing orange.

As it ages, cheese mites, which the French call little affineurs, are allowed onto the rind. They eat into the crust, leaving the grey, pitted, moon-like surface, and help the cheese ripen. In 2013 the American FDA detained about a ton of Mimolette because the mites exceeded six per cubic inch; the restriction was lifted in 2014.

Today a large maker is the Normandy cooperative Isigny Sainte-Mère, which began making Mimolette, also called Boule de Lille, in 1951 with master cheesemakers recruited from the north, and sells it from young to extra-mature at 24 months.

What Americans call a Castelvetrano olive is, strictly, a way of preparing an olive. The variety is Nocellara del Belice, grown in the Valle del Belice in south-western Sicily, a dual-purpose olive pressed for oil and cured for the table. One of its table preparations is named for the comune of Castelvetrano in the valley, and olives treated that way are sold in the United States as Castelvetrano olives.

In 1817 Girolamo Luxardo moved to Zara, on the Dalmatian coast, as consular representative of the Kingdom of Sardinia. His wife, Maria Canevari, made rosolio maraschino at home, a cherry liqueur of the region, and in 1821 he founded a distillery to make it properly. Within eight years the Emperor recognised it as superior. The war ended all of it. Allied bombing from November 1943 to October 1944 destroyed 80 per cent of Zara, and the factory with it. Pietro Luxardo and his brother Nicolò, with Nicolò's wife, were killed by Tito's partisans. Giorgio Luxardo, the only survivor of the fourth generation, fled across the Adriatic; the family story says he carried a single cherry sapling.

With Nicolò III of the fifth generation he re-founded the firm briefly in Venice, then at Torreglia in the Euganean Hills near Padua, where the first marasca orchard was planted in 1947. It now has 20,000 trees, the company is still family owned, and it marked 200 years in 2021.

Burrata is a fresh cheese of the Murgia in Puglia, made from cow's milk, rennet and cream: a pouch of mozzarella filled with shreds of curd soaked in cream. Its birthplace is the town of Andria, though the date is argued. Some place it about 1900, at the farm of the brothers Lorenzo and Vincenzo Bianchino; more recent records credit Lorenzo Bianchino of the Piana Padura farm with first making it in 1956.

The story told in Puglia is of a heavy February snowfall that kept Bianchino from the market. With milk that would not keep, he wrapped curd, scraps of mozzarella and the cream from the morning milking inside a skin of mozzarella, so nothing was wasted.

For decades it stayed a local fresh cheese that had to be eaten within days. In November 2016 Burrata di Andria became a protected geographical indication, an IGP, recognising the town's claim.

On the Creole Tomato Tostada it does what mozzarella does in a caprese: a cool, milky foil for raw Louisiana tomatoes, torn and served at room temperature.

Sherry is the fortified wine of a triangle of towns in the province of Cádiz, in southern Spain: Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María. It is made mostly from the Palomino grape, in styles from pale, salty Manzanilla and fino to the darker Amontillado and oloroso, which age in contact with air and turn nutty and deep.

What makes Sherry is the way it ages, criaderas y solera. Barrels are stacked in tiers; wine for bottling is drawn from the oldest, which is topped up from the next oldest, and so on up to the youngest. Every bottle is a blend of many years, and the style stays the same from decade to decade. That ageing was long reserved to the three towns.

In 1933 Jerez became the first denominación de origen recognised under Spain's new wine law, D.O. Jerez-Xeres-Sherry, though Rioja, which set up its own in 1925, also claims to be first.

Brennan's has finished its turtle soup with sherry for a long time: its own published recipe calls for dry sherry and hard-boiled egg, and says the flavour is heightened by a touch of sherry. Tonight's menu prints aged Sherry, and which bottle the kitchen uses is a question for lineup.

Gulf fish on a New Orleans menu means the day's catch, not one species. The city's appetite runs to fish such as true American red snapper and black drum, which sell far above the national average here, and sheepshead, an estuarine fish of Louisiana's coast that is nearly all sold to restaurants and markets in the state.

Louisiana has worked to widen that list. In 1981 the legislature created the Louisiana Seafood Promotion and Marketing Board to promote the state's commercial catch, with particular attention to underused species.

Brennan's owner has a public record on Gulf seafood. After the 2010 BP oil spill Ralph Brennan testified before Congress about the damage to the Gulf seafood industry, and he advocates sustainable, local seafood sourcing in each of his restaurants. In New Orleans the Audubon Nature Institute runs GULF, a sustainable seafood programme founded in 2012 that works with restaurants and fisheries.

Turtle soup has been eaten in Louisiana since the 1700s, and it is still on the menus of the old houses: Arnaud's, Commander's Palace, Mandina's, Felix's and Brennan's among them. At Brennan's the chefs use snappers, freshwater snapping turtles.

The rules on which snapper changed in 2004. The alligator snapping turtle, the great loggerhead once common in Louisiana markets, became off limits to commercial trappers when a Wildlife and Fisheries regulation took effect on 20 November 2004. Licensed turtle farmers may still sell alligator snappers hatched from their own breeding stock, and Commander's Palace uses farm-raised alligator snapper for a steady supply. The common snapping turtle could still be taken and sold by holders of a reptile and amphibian collection licence, by a 2017 account, and most of the state's turtle trade involves farm-hatched animals.

For cooks, Brennan's own published turtle soup recipe notes that fresh or frozen turtle meat can be bought from specialty markets and seafood dealers in and around New Orleans. Brennan's menu prints 100% turtle meat, which means the meat in the soup is all turtle, not stretched with veal or beef. It does not say which snapper or which supplier.

Tien Dat is a small local tofu maker, part of the VEGGI Farmers Cooperative, whose extra firm tofu reaches the city through the co-op. Two Brooks Farm sits at Sumner in the Mississippi Delta. Mike Wagner started it in 1992, and he is a ninth-generation farmer: his family counts an unbroken line of ten generations back to 1742. The farm grows about 2,000 acres of rice and 1,000 of soybeans.

What sets it apart is the birds. The farm lies on the flyway, and after harvest ducks and geese settle on the flooded fields. Wagner noticed his soil changing where they gathered and began cutting back on fertiliser; the birds now supply much of it, and no fungicides or insecticides go on the rice.

From that long-grain rice the family built a line of 14 products, rice, grits and flour among them, with the Original Mississippi Midlands Brown Rice Grits one of Wagner's favourites. His son Lawrence and daughter Abbey, the next generation, have helped widen the range, and the products reach restaurants through US Foods. In 2022 Wagner was named Mississippi's winner of the Swisher Sweets/Sunbelt Ag Expo Southeastern Farmer of the Year award.

In 1923 Alvin A. Baumer borrowed money from his future in-laws and bought Mill's Fruit Products, a small snow-cone syrup company on Tchoupitoulas Street. Tucked in a drawer was a recipe for a pepper sauce labelled Crystal Pure. Baumer renamed it Crystal Pure Louisiana Hot Sauce and began bottling it in the city.

For decades Baumer Foods was as much a maker of jellies, preserves and mustard as of hot sauce. From the 1940s it bottled Crystal on Tulane Avenue, where a neon sign of a chef stirring a steaming pot of strawberry jam became a local landmark. The flooding after Hurricane Katrina in 2005 ruined that plant and forced the company to drop its historic preserves, jellies and mustard; it moved upriver to Reserve, Louisiana, at the Port of South Louisiana, 9 feet above sea level.

The recipe is short: aged red cayenne peppers, distilled vinegar and salt, giving a reddish orange sauce with medium heat. The company is still family owned, led by Alvin "Al" Baumer Jr.

changes.before:
Creole is a growers' word before it is a variety. Farmers in St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes traditionally sold their tomatoes as Creole, and said that ripening on the vine in rich alluvial river soil gave them a flavour no other Louisiana or American tomato had. In the early 1900s, before tomatoes carried variety names, fruit from St. Charles, St. John and St. James parishes was simply called Creole too.

The LSU AgCenter muddied the water in 1969, when researcher Teme Hernandez released a variety actually named Creole. It yielded poorly, less than six pounds a plant, was never common in St. Bernard or Plaquemines, and the AgCenter did not keep its seed. So a Creole tomato today is a Louisiana-grown tomato picked ripe, not one cultivar.

The city celebrates it every June at the French Market's Creole Tomato Festival, which began in 1985 to mark the start of the season and honours the farmers who grow them. The French Market itself has stood since 1791.

Louisiana cane syrup is cane juice concentrated by long cooking in open kettles, with nothing taken out and nothing added. Slow Food lists traditional cane syrup on its Ark of Taste, the catalogue of heritage foods worth saving.

The name most Louisianans reach for is Steen's. In 1910 an early freeze hit Charley Steen's cane crop near Abbeville. Rather than lose it, he built a small mill and turned the frozen cane into a few barrels of syrup. By 1930 Charley and Elizabeth Steen and their children had built a larger mill in the heart of Abbeville, on the banks of Bayou Vermilion, and from the 1950s the yellow can became a fixture of Cajun and Creole kitchens. The mill is still run by the Steen family and still cooks in open kettles, which is why the label reads 100% Pure Cane Syrup.

Brennan's menu prints cane syrup on the peaches of the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast but names no maker, so Steen's is the story of the style, not a claim about the kitchen's bottle.

Louisiana is one of the few states where the pecan is native. The state holds between 19,000 and 21,000 acres of native trees, and their nuts tend to be small, flavourful and high in oil, unlike the larger improved varieties bred since. The LSU AgCenter runs the only university research station in the country devoted solely to pecans.

The improved pecan itself began in Louisiana. In the winter of 1846 or 1847, Antoine, an enslaved gardener at Oak Alley Plantation in St. James Parish, grafted pecan wood from a tree with large, thin-shelled nuts onto other trees. He grafted sixteen trees near the house, more were grafted later, and by the end of the Civil War in 1865 Oak Alley had 126 grafted trees in bearing. His nut, later named Centennial, won a prize at the 1876 Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia, and grafting made the pecan an orchard crop.

In New Orleans kitchens the pecan stands where the almond stood in French recipes. It runs right through Brennan's menus: the pecan bordelaise on the Pecan Gulf Fish, the oat and pecan crumble on the Baked Apple, the pecans on the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake and the pralines on the bread pudding.

The praline began as a French sugared almond, named for César, duc de Choiseul, comte du Plessis-Praslin, whose chef made it. Early in the eighteenth century the Ursuline nuns are credited with bringing the candy to New Orleans.

The New Orleans praline is a different thing, and it was made by the city's Black women. They took the almond sweet, used the pecans that grew all around them and added milk or cream, turning a hard sugared nut into the soft, creamy patty the city knows.

In the mid to late nineteenth century, women called pralinières sold them on the streets of the French Quarter. Free women of colour and enslaved women alike made and sold them, and for Black women it was a way to earn their own money; some bought their own freedom and their families' with the proceeds. On Brennan's New Orleans Bread Pudding, pralines bring that history and a caramel crunch to the whiskey caramel and buttermilk ice cream.

changes.before:
South Louisiana Rice Dressing carries its place in its name. Rice growing on the southwest Louisiana prairie began in earnest in the early 1880s, and by 1890 a record crop of 80 million pounds made Louisiana the leading rice state, overtaking South Carolina. Crowley, the seat of Acadia Parish, became the centre of the industry, its fields watered by canals and wells.

Between 1800 and 1920 the region changed from subsistence farming and open-range cattle country into the first mechanised commercial rice region in the world, and southwest Louisiana still holds nearly 500,000 acres of rice land.

That is why rice, not bread, is the stuffing of south Louisiana: rice dressing is cooked rice folded into browned meat and the holy trinity, a Sunday and holiday dish. Brennan's prints the side with no description and no rice brand, so the meats and the rice are questions for the kitchen.

Tasso belongs to the boucherie, the communal hog butchering of Acadiana, where neighbours killed a pig together and shared every part. The boucherie gave the Cajun larder boudin, cracklin', andouille and tasso, and tasso was traditionally made from the last lean pieces: a seasoning meat, not a meal.

It is often called a ham, but the name misleads. Tasso is cut from the shoulder, not the hind leg. The shoulder is sliced across the grain into pieces about three inches thick, cured briefly in salt and sugar for only three or four hours, rinsed, rubbed with cayenne and garlic, and hot-smoked until cooked through. The smokehouse has its own Acadian French word, boucanière.

Cooks rarely eat tasso on its own. They dice it into jambalaya, stews and braised vegetables, where a little carries smoke, salt and heat through the pot. At Brennan's it seasons the Creole sauce of the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits. The menu names no maker, so who smokes it is a question for the kitchen.

Sazerac Rye carries the name of a bar. In the 1850s the Sazerac Coffee House in New Orleans took its name from Sazerac de Forge et Fils cognac, which by the company's account went into its house cocktail. Thomas H. Handy took over the coffee house in 1869, and as phylloxera ruined the European vineyards, rye whiskey took the cognac's place in the city's drink.

The bottle is the Sazerac Company's namesake straight rye, distilled at Buffalo Trace in Frankfort, Kentucky, and bottled at 90 proof. It was once labelled 6 years old and now carries no age statement; the mash bill is not disclosed, and it shares its grain recipe with Sazerac 18 Year and Thomas H. Handy. Reviewers find it light bodied for a rye, with apricot, orange peel, caramel and vanilla over the pepper.

The company grew from Handy's firm, which also came to own Antoine Peychaud's bitters. It was reorganised as the Sazerac Company in 1919, rode out Prohibition as a grocery wholesaler, and in 1948 was bought by Magnolia Liquor, a New Orleans wholesaler founded by two partners; the family of one of them owns it still. It bought Herbsaint in 1949 and the distillery now called Buffalo Trace in 1992, and it remains privately held, headquartered in Metairie, with more than 500 brands. All three bottles of the Classic Sazerac are its own.

In 2019 it opened the Sazerac House at the corner of Canal and Magazine, a museum with a small still that makes Sazerac rye.

Herbsaint was born in New Orleans in 1934, just after the repeal of Prohibition, while absinthe was still banned in the United States, as it had been since 1912. Its makers were J. Marion Legendre and Reginald Parker, who had learnt absinthe making in France during the First World War.

Legendre first sold it as Legendre Absinthe, though it never held grand wormwood. Within months the Federal Alcohol Control Administration objected to the word absinthe, and he renamed it Herbsaint, from herbe sainte, the Creole name for wormwood. In time it became a usual rinse for the Sazerac, the city's own cocktail.

In June 1949 the Sazerac Company, the New Orleans firm behind Sazerac Rye and Peychaud's, bought J.M. Legendre and Co. In the mid-1950s the standard bottling became a different 90 proof recipe, and by the early 1970s it was the only Herbsaint made. In December 2009, for the brand's 75th anniversary, the company brought back Legendre's original 100 proof recipe as Herbsaint Original. Both are sold today, and the 90 proof remains the predominant bottling.

The company does not say where Herbsaint is made now, so it is described as born in New Orleans, not made there.

Rittenhouse Rye was first sold in Philadelphia in 1934, just after Prohibition, by Continental Distilling, and named for the city's Rittenhouse Square. In 1948 it was relaunched as a four-year-old bottled in bond rye, the form it keeps. Heaven Hill bought the brand in the 1990s, in 1993 by some accounts and 1999 by others, and moved its production from Pennsylvania to Kentucky.

Heaven Hill itself was founded at Bardstown in 1935 by a group of investors; in time five brothers of one family bought out the rest, and their descendants own and run the company still. On 7 November 1996 fire swept through its warehouses, and some 90,000 barrels burned. In 1999 it bought the Bernheim distillery in Louisville, where it has distilled since, while ageing and bottling stayed around Bardstown; a new Bardstown distillery filled its first barrel on 7 April 2025.

Bottled in bond means the spirit of a single distilling season, aged at least four years in a federally bonded warehouse and bottled at 100 proof. Rittenhouse is 51 percent rye, with corn and malted barley: a modern Kentucky recipe, lower in rye than the old Pennsylvania ryes it nods to.

Rumors are Flying prints Brennan's Barrel Aged Rittenhouse Rye. No public source says what that means: a barrel chosen for the house, or rye rested again in a cask of the bar's own. The bar holds that story.

Rabbit Hole was founded in Louisville in 2012 by a former clinical psychologist who left the profession to distil whiskey. The name, by one account, comes from his wife's warning that the venture would take the family down a rabbit hole from which they could never return. She is a Louisville native and a bourbon lover who had drawn him from Scotch to bourbon, and Dareringer, the sherry-finished bourbon, is named in her honour.

In its first years the brand's whiskey was made at other distilleries while its own was designed and built. The distillery opened in May 2018 in downtown Louisville. In June 2019 Pernod Ricard USA agreed to buy a majority share, at a price never disclosed; at the time the founder kept most of his shares and stayed on to run the company.

Dareringer is a wheated Kentucky straight bourbon. It ages first in new charred American oak, then is finished in casks that held Pedro Ximénez, a dark and very sweet sherry, and it is bottled at 93 proof. The finish lays raisin and dried fruit richness over the bourbon's vanilla and oak, a richness that carries the smoke, the Angostura, the orange and the cherry of the Birdcage.

Jade Nouvelle-Orléans is the work of Jade Liqueurs, a company founded in 2000 by a New Orleans-born scientist and absinthe historian. He researched surviving pre-ban absinthes and the old methods of making them, aiming to recreate the spirit as it was before the bans of the early twentieth century, without the myths that had grown up around it. Nouvelle-Orléans was the first Jade absinthe; a specialist retailer dates it to 2004 and says the founder has personally produced every batch since.

It is made at the Combier distillery in Saumur, in the Loire Valley, chosen partly for its historic equipment: copper bain-marie alembics built in the 1870s and acquired from one of the original absinthe distilleries of Pontarlier, France. Wormwood and other plants are macerated in wine alcohol and distilled, and a second infusion of plants in the distillate gives the pale green colour. It is bottled at 68 percent.

The name is a tribute to the founder's home city and its nineteenth-century absinthe culture. Its sellers describe the style as rooted in the absinthes that made the Sazerac and the Absinthe Frappé famous: fresh, with a peppery spice.

At Brennan's it is printed only on the Origin Story, the top of the Sazerac ladder, beside Dudognon Cognac and barrel-aged Peychaud's.

St. George Spirits was founded in 1982 as an eau de vie distillery, making clear fruit brandies. Its founder was master distiller for 28 years before handing the role to his successor in 2010. In 2004 the company moved into a 65,000-square-foot aircraft hangar on the former Alameda Naval Air Station, where it still distils.

When absinthe returned to American shelves in 2007, once federal regulators accepted that a properly made one met the thujone limit, St. George had a recipe ready, developed over eleven years. The label office refused the label several times, objecting to the monkey on it and to the word Verte, before approving it in early December 2007. St. George Absinthe Verte went on sale on 21 December 2007, the first legal American-made absinthe in 95 years, and the first 1,800 bottles sold out in six hours.

It is built on brandy rather than the beet spirit of many absinthes. Wormwood, fennel and star anise are infused in the brandy and distilled; the distillate is then infused with mint, tarragon, Genovese basil, lemon balm, hyssop and stinging nettle, which give the green colour and a garden character. Star anise is itself a departure from the green anise of the classic European recipes. It is bottled at 60 percent.

At Brennan's it rinses the glass of Thompson's Dream, the first step up from the Classic Sazerac, in place of the Classic's Herbsaint.

Louis-Napoléon Mattei opened his first shop in Bastia, on Corsica, in 1872, selling cigars, coffee, wine and liqueurs. In 1874 he began distilling cédrat, the thick-skinned citron of Cap Corse, the island's northern peninsula, and in 1875 he made a medicinal wine with quinquina, the cinchona bark that gives quinine. Accounts differ on how he came to the bark: his importer says he found it on a voyage to the Caribbean; another source says he meant it against malaria.

The Blanc is a mistelle: Muscat and Vermentinu grape must kept from fermenting with neutral alcohol, so its sweetness is the grape's own. It is flavoured with cinchona, cédrat and other plants, fruits and spices, and bottled at 17 percent. The bark brings spice and gentle bitterness to the middle and finish; the cédrat brings citrus perfume and a silky texture.

Its American importer has long called the house family owned, with macerations, ageing and bottling done in house, by one report in the Borgo industrial zone. Monocle reports, though, that a Corsican drinks group, Groupe Boisson Corse, has since bought the house, revived the founder's recipe and taken output from about 80,000 bottles to about 400,000. On Cap Corse stands the Moulin Mattei, a windmill a later head of the house turned into an advertisement for the aperitif; the Conservatoire du Littoral bought it in 2004 and restored its 1930s look.

At Brennan's it plays the vermouth's part in the Spoonbill, with Hendrick's gin and chive oil.

Nocello is made by Toschi, a family company founded in 1945 in Vignola, near Modena, by two brothers. They began by preserving cherries in spirit, and the company still specialises in fruit in spirit, liqueurs and products for gelato. Its working headquarters are now at Savignano sul Panaro, close by.

Nocello is made from walnuts and hazelnuts. It is amber, sweet and rounded, with a balanced walnut flavour and tones of vanilla, and bottled at 24 percent; in 2004 it won a gold medal at the IWSC. In the United States its label reads Imitation Liqueur. Toschi has not published its method, so a server describes the taste, not a process.

It belongs to the walnut liqueur tradition of Emilia-Romagna, whose best-known member is nocino, the dark liqueur made by steeping green walnuts in alcohol; by custom the walnuts are picked around St John's Day, 24 June. Toschi makes a Nocino too. Nocello is the lighter, sweeter cousin.

At Brennan's it goes into Ralph’s Coffee, with dark roast coffee and chicory, Frangelico and whipped cream: a roasty, nutty after-dinner coffee.

Allspice dram, called pimento dram in Jamaica, is rum in which allspice berries have been steeped, then sweetened. Allspice is the dried berry of the pimento tree; the Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails says its flavour recalls cloves, cinnamon and nutmeg, and records the dram as an article of commerce since the 1850s. Bottles were shown at the International Exhibition of 1862. In Jamaica the berry kept its Spanish name, pimiento, now pimento; the English called it allspice. It is no relation of the pimento pepper.

The National Museum Jamaica records that the liqueur became popular in Europe and North America in the early 1900s, when J. Wray & Nephew bottled and sold it. It appeared in drinks such as the Lion's Tail and was taken up by the tiki bars. Imports to the United States later stopped, and bartenders made their own.

The revival came in 2008 with St. Elizabeth Allspice Dram, made in Austria from Jamaican allspice berries, raw sugar and pot-stilled Jamaican rum for an American importer.

At Brennan's it gives For Sentimental Reasons its warm baking spice, under pear purée and sparkling wine. The menu names no brand, so which dram the bar pours is a lineup question.

Chopin is a Polish vodka named for the composer Frédéric Chopin, a favoured son of Poland. It is made by Podlaska Wytwórnia Wódek Polmos of Siedlce, east of Warsaw, at a distillery near the hamlet of Krzesk that has made vodka since 1896. The brand says its still of that year is one of the oldest remaining stills in Poland.

The brand dates from the early 1990s: sources give 1992 or 1993. When its founder bought the distillery itself is less clear: one account says 1993, another 2003. Chopin reached North America in 1997. The company calls itself family owned and run, now in its second generation, and Poland’s last family owned vodka brand.

Chopin is a single-ingredient vodka. Each bottling is made from one raw material, potato, rye or wheat, and distilled four times. The brand grows some of its ingredients on its own farmland and buys the rest from family farms near the distillery, and its water comes from an artesian spring beneath the grounds. The potato vodka, the best known bottling, uses Stobrawa potatoes, which retailers say are grown in Podlasie.

Potato vodka is fuller and creamier in texture than most grain vodkas, with a faint earthiness. Which Chopin goes into the Flamingo is a question for the bar.

Monkey 47 tells its own story through a British officer. By the brand’s account, Montgomery Collins, known as Monty, a Royal Air Force officer posted to Berlin after the Second World War, sponsored a monkey named Max at the Berlin Zoo. He left the air force in 1951, settled in the northern Black Forest and opened a guesthouse, Zum Wilden Affen, the Wild Monkey, where his Schwarzwald Dry Gin was the house drink until the 1970s. No archive or independent account of him has been found, so it is told as the brand’s story.

The modern gin began in 2008, when the founder, from a German brandy family, left a job at Nokia to recreate the recipe in the Black Forest. After more than 120 trial distillations the gin came to market, usually dated 2010. In January 2016 Pernod Ricard Deutschland agreed to buy a majority stake, and in March 2020 Pernod Ricard bought the rest, with the founder staying on as an adviser. The distillery near Loßburg, built in 2015, centres on a custom still from a German coppersmith.

The name holds the numbers: 47 botanicals and 47 percent alcohol. About a third of the botanicals are Black Forest plants, among them spruce, lingonberries, elderflower, blackthorn and bramble leaves, and the citrus peels go in fresh. They macerate in molasses-based neutral spirit and spring water before distillation in small stills; the gin then rests in large earthenware vessels for about three months, is cut slowly with water and is bottled without chill filtration.

Hendrick’s is a Scottish gin made by William Grant & Sons, the family-owned company William Grant founded in 1887, the year his Glenfiddich distillery began production, and still run by his descendants. The gin is made at Girvan, where the company built its grain distillery in 1963 under a great-grandson of William Grant.

That same great-grandson bought two old stills at auction in 1966: a Bennett still of 1860 and a Carter-Head still built in 1948 by John Dore & Co. By the company’s account, in 1988 he set a company distiller the task of making one spirit from both. After years of trials Hendrick’s launched in 1999: the gins of the two stills are blended, then essences of rose and cucumber are added. Because the rose and cucumber go in after distillation, it cannot be labelled a London Dry gin.

Eleven botanicals stand behind the rose and cucumber, among them juniper, orris root, chamomile, cubeb, elderflower, yarrow, caraway and lemon and orange peel. The rose is described as Bulgarian; the cucumbers come from Holland or Belgium. The name, by most accounts, was chosen by a member of the Grant family after Hendrick, a gardener who took particular care of the family’s roses.

On 1 October 2018 the company opened the Hendrick’s Gin Palace in the grounds at Girvan, with new still houses that doubled capacity and glasshouses of exotic botanicals.

Seven Three Distilling Co. is a New Orleans craft distillery named for the city’s 73 officially recognised neighbourhoods, and it names its spirits after them: St. Roch Vodka, Bywater Bourbon, Marigny Moonshine, Irish Channel Whiskey, Black Pearl Rum and Gentilly Gin. A New Orleans husband and wife developed the brand while building a custom distillery, which opened in early 2017 in a warehouse at 301 North Claiborne Avenue, on the corner of Bienville Street, usually described as Tremé. Its first release was a run of 1,000 bottles of St. Roch Vodka, a neutral spirit redistilled and filtered for five days through copper, limestone and charcoal.

Gentilly Gin starts from the same neutral base. Juniper is joined by persimmon and elderflower, 17 botanicals in all, inspired by the traiteurs, the old faith healers of Louisiana. It is bottled at 87 proof, 43.5 percent. Tasters find elderflower, a little anise and vanilla on the nose, honeyed persimmon, ginger and juniper on the palate, and a peppery finish. A Barrel Reserve version rests in barrels before bottling.

Gentilly itself is one of the city’s old neighbourhoods. By the common account, in 1727 the colonists Mathurin and Pierre Dreux chose the natural levee along Bayou Sauvage for their plantation and named it after the French community they came from; one recent history argues the name began as Chantilly.

Cathead Distillery was founded in 2010 by two friends and blues fans who had spent about eleven years working in South Carolina before coming home to Jackson, Mississippi. Mississippi passed statewide prohibition in 1907 and was the last state to repeal it, in 1966, and then only county by county; the founders had to help amend several old state laws before they could open. Cathead went to market in May 2010, and Visit Jackson and the company’s own releases call it Mississippi’s first legal distillery.

It began in Gluckstadt and moved downtown to 422 South Farish Street in 2015. The name is blues slang: the old blues players called each other cats, as a term of respect. The logo draws on the folk art of the Delta bluesman James Son Thomas, who sculpted cat heads from river clay, and the company has sent part of its sales to music nonprofits.

Cathead makes vodkas, Bristow Gin, a chicory liqueur called Hoodoo and Old Soul Bourbon in small batches. Its vodka is made in runs of 500 gallons or less, with some sweet corn in the grain for a crisp finish, and bottled at 80 proof. Beside the plain vodka come flavoured ones: honeysuckle, pecan, a bitter orange made with bitter orange and satsuma extracts, and a Satsuma Mandarin Vodka listed on the distillery’s shop pages, most likely the bottle the menu calls Cathead Mandarin Vodka. No source gives its proof or how it is flavoured; a canned Satsuma Mandarin vodka soda at 5 percent is a different product.

Volcán De Mi Tierra, the volcano of my land, is a tequila house born of a partnership between Moët Hennessy, the wine and spirits arm of LVMH, and a Mexican family whose lineage in Mexico goes back to the seventeenth century. By the brand’s story, a meeting between a family elder and LVMH executives raised the question of why the group had no tequila. The family owned land and a small distillery near the long-dormant Tequila Volcano in Jalisco; the partners chose the distillery, NOM 1523, revamped it and revived a brand the family had called Volcán. It has been described as the first 50:50 partnership LVMH had entered.

The tequila launched on 1 May 2017 with a Blanco and a Cristalino, a blend of añejo and extra añejo tequilas filtered clear, in eight American cities and Mexico. In October 2025 it was named the Official Tequila of Formula 1 under LVMH’s ten-year deal with the series.

The brand says the volcano’s ash left a soil rich in basalt and iron, which gives the tequila its taste. The agave comes from two terroirs: the highlands, at about 1,700 metres on iron-rich red clay, and the lowlands, at about 1,000 metres on dark volcanic soil that gives earthier, spicier notes. The Reposado rests in American and European oak, 135 days by one account and nine months by another, and is bottled at 40 percent: honey, dried fruit, toasted nuts, oak and vanilla.

Taittinger traces its start to 1734, when Jacques Fourneaux began trading Champagne wines and worked with the Benedictine abbeys that owned some of the best vineyards. In the 1820s the firm became Forest-Fourneaux, and in 1932 Pierre Taittinger bought it and gave it his name; one source gives 1931.

In the years from 1945 to 1960 the house set up its cellars in the Gallo-Roman chalk pits beneath the site of the Saint-Nicaise abbey in Reims, where the wines still age. In 2005 the family sold its group to the American fund Starwood Capital Group; in 2006 a family-led bid, backed by the bank Crédit Agricole, bought the Champagne house back. A member of the family has been president since 1 January 2020.

Brut La Française is the house’s non-vintage Brut. Its mark is a high share of Chardonnay for a non-vintage blend, about 40 percent, with Pinot Noir and Meunier, which gives the light, fresh, elegant style the house is known for. One reviewer says it spends a year longer on its lees than the Brut Réserve, which ages at least three years.

At Brennan’s it tops the Flamingo in the Roost, and the same wine sits on the Birthday Bubbles list as a 3 litre double magnum.

Elio Perrone is a family estate in Castiglione Tinella, in the Moscato hills of the province of Asti in Piedmont. Sources say the family has made Moscato there since the end of the nineteenth century, over four generations. One profile dates the present generation’s taking over to 1989, when the son of the man whose name is on the label took the reins; another says the father retired in the late 1990s.

Moscato is the heart of the estate’s production. The family also farms vines at Isola d’Asti, where Barbera leads and Brachetto grows too, and the present generation created Bigaro, a blend of the two aromatic grapes made in the style of Moscato d’Asti.

Bigaro is its pink, softly sparkling wine: half Brachetto and half Moscato, crushed together and left a few days on the skins, with the fermentation stopped by filtering, so that it keeps some grape sugar and a light fizz at about 5 percent alcohol; one listing gives 7 percent for the 2024. Brachetto brings red berries and rose, Moscato brings peach and orange blossom, and the colour is salmon. Its importer lists it as Piedmont DOC, and it is served well chilled, as an aperitif or with fruit desserts.

In the OBX it tops Gentilly Gin, peach and lemon, adding fruit, a soft sweetness and a gentle sparkle.

Wölffer Estate began with Christian Wölffer, a German-born investor who bought farmland at Sagaponack, on Long Island, from 1978, first for a horse farm. The original vineyard, acquired in 1988, had been a potato field. The winery was founded as Sagpond Vineyards in 1987 or 1988, by different accounts, and later renamed Wölffer Estate Vineyard, in 1997 by one account, when a new winery opened. Its winemaker came from Germany in 1992 and is now a partner. Christian Wölffer died on New Year’s Eve 2008 in Brazil, and the estate is owned and run by his children with that partner. It is known above all for its rosé.

Wölffer began making non-alcoholic drinks in 1996, with verjus. In 2021 it launched Spring in a Bottle, a non-alcoholic sparkling rosé made in Germany from a certified organic vineyard in Rheinhessen, with the alcohol and other volatiles gently removed at a low 77°F. It also sells Petite Rosé, a sparkling drink pressed from unripe grapes, and a still Summer in a Bottle Rosé Zero.

A dealcoholised wine is made as wine first and then stripped of its alcohol: by vacuum distillation at low temperature, by a spinning cone column, which takes off the lightest aromas first and blends them back, or by reverse osmosis through fine membranes. Wölffer does not say which method it uses.
